#3411. Blade Runner 2099 Review: Hunter Schafer And Michelle Yeoh Star In The Best Sci-Fi Show In Years

In the case of the "Blade Runner" franchise, the future seems to arrive right on time. It's no coincidence that both films in the series were made during periods of severe social and political anxiety in America, with their dystopias not just predicting our future but reflecting our present. Although Ridley Scott's 1982 masterpiece is still generally well regarded, it also feels a little underrated in terms of how massively influential it was. It not only still casts a shadow over the science fiction genre, but began a trend within Hollywood of more filmmakers utilizing the works of author Philip K. Dick, whose novel "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?" served as the source material. It was instrumental in kicking off the cyberpunk subgenre, with so many tech-centric dystopias following in its wake. Meanwhile, Denis Villeneuve's decades-later sequel "Blade Runner 2049" is a masterwork in its own right, a sequel which has itself inspired pop culture.

As we endure this latest period of anxiety, along comes a new "Blade Runner" to mirror our malaise. We're in a particularly fertile period for dark sci-fi to emerge, with everything from the rise of AI to the failure of governmental and technical systems occurring around us. As such, it feels fitting that this new "Blade Runner" isn't another movie, but an 8-episode series: "Blade Runner 2099." As the title suggests, this isn't some lazy continuation, but is instead a leap forward within the series' parallel universe in which artificial humans known as Replicants exist. Showrunner Silka Luisa has put together something that's as unique and bold as it is in conversation with its franchise's past, making it a proud new addition to the saga. In many ways, "Blade Runner 2099" is the best sci-fi show in years.

"Blade Runner 2099" introduces us to the surprisingly sunny but still noir-ish Los Angeles of 2099, a city which feels like Ridley Scott's overcrowded metropolis and Denis Villeneuve's stark landscapes have been merged. More than just paying homage to the past, this provides a fitting backdrop to an LA which exists after the Replicant uprising (which was hinted at toward the end of "2049"). Now the script has been flipped: Replicants are the dominant species on Earth, having subjugated the remaining humans. Those humans who cannot go (or are not sent) off-world occupy menial jobs, and any who exhibit resistance are retired by Replicant Blade Runners.

After the human Cora (Hunter Schafer) gets caught in a Blade Runner raid at her job where she's forced to run, she tries to use a human sympathizer, Bebeto (Dimitri Abold) to help her and her disabled brother Elias (Lewis Gribben) get to Mexico City, the last city on Earth where humanity has true freedom. Bebeto needs Cora to do something for him in exchange, which is to pose as a Replicant (and a Blade Runner) in order to obtain an object from LAPD lockup.

Upon attempting this, Cora is suddenly assigned to work with Olwen (Michelle Yeoh), a veteran Blade Runner whose predetermined Replicant death time is coming up shortly. With that, the series is off on its own unique sci-fi/noir trip. While there are several callbacks to prior elements of the franchise (things like the Voight-Kampff test and the JOI device make an appearance), these are part of its worldbuilding more than any fan service. "2099" is unquestionably a part of "Blade Runner," yet its reconfiguring of the world allows it to stand alone, too.

Right away, the franchise's themes of identity, existentialism, and morality come to the fore in the series, all of which showrunner Silka Luisa and company explore with aplomb. A big part of why it feels so fresh lies in the show's female leads, a development which feels natural rather than belabored.

Though the themes of "Blade Runner" have always been universal, the first two films do have notably masculine viewpoints. Here, Hunter Schafer and Michelle Yeoh bring a new feminine energy to the franchise which feels distinct from the men in the franchise but also from the previous films' women. Yeoh's extensive history with the action genre makes Olwen's strength almost second nature, while Schafer builds upon her excellent work in "Cuckoo" by making Cora a woman who is also slowly getting more and more in over her head. These layered characterizations are helped by the series' scripts, which are of a idiosyncratic, sci-fi-forward quality worthy of the franchise.

As great as the performances and writing are, the folks behind "Blade Runner 2099" are well aware that a large part of the series' fame is due to its visual design, and as such the series has not skimped in that department. "2099" utilizes its status as a series to take us to many more places in the "Blade Runner" universe than just LA and the surrounding areas, and the production design goes beyond Scott and Villeneuve as influences. In fact, one sequence feels worthy of mentioning in the same breath as Andrei Tarkovsky. Meanwhile, the series' cinematographers (led by Rob Hardy) maintain a consistently strong level of quality over the episodes, while composer Leopold Ross builds a hypnotically strange sonic tapestry that never reuses old themes.

"Blade Runner 2099" is one of those shows that leaves you awed at how they managed to accomplish so much with it. If there is a flaw within, it's the usual issue with so many streaming series these days, which is that some story beats (and a few whole scenes) feel unnecessarily lengthened and padded out. It's also a shame that Prime Video is releasing the show all at once, as it feels like the series was produced to foster a week-to-week audience (similar to "Crystal Lake" from last month), and, given its rich material, could've likely grown one. That aside, "Blade Runner 2099" is a show that has a lot going for it, not the least of which is its intelligence and imagination.

It carries on the concepts and themes of Philip K. Dick while adding some wild new ideas. Its closest cousin in this way may be another Ridley Scott-backed series, the underseen "Raised By Wolves." Given its boldness, one wonders if the 8 episodes of "2099" are intended as the final word, both for itself and for "Blade Runner" in general. Whatever the future holds, I believe the show is the best sci-fi IP revival since Ronald D. Moore's "Battlestar Galactica." It's that intriguing, that layered, and that vibrant. In keeping with the original film's reputation, the various interpretations that the series' ending invites are enough to keep the show worth talking about for years to come. It may have been almost a decade since "2049," but "Blade Runner 2099" has arrived right on time.

"Blade Runner 2099" premieres November 25, 2026 on Prime Video.

Hallmark churns out nearly a hundred new romance movies every year. The 2026 Countdown to Christmas lineup alone is slated for 34 original holiday-themed flicks. Part of the reason it’s easy for the cable channel-turned-streamer to make so many movies a year is that it has a list of dedicated actors who are eager to star in these films -- like Queen of Hallmark Lacey Chabert. And yet, somehow, they manage to keep the pairings fresh. So fresh that two of my favorite longtime Hallmark actors, Erin Cahill and Andrew Walker, just starred in their first movie together. I’m happy to report it was worth the wait!

Yep, you read that right. After spending 20 years with the cable channel and being friends for 18 years, Cahill and Walker finally got to share the screen as romantic leads in Christmas in Blue Dog Valley. The holiday flick follows Goldie MacKenzie (Cahil), a former Hollywood on-set veterinarian, who decides to leave the glitz and glamour for a slower life as the in-house veterinarian in the small town of Blue Dog Valley.

The residents of Blue Dog Valley aren’t too thrilled about an outsider taking over their beloved veterinary practice, and Goldie has to work overtime to win over the hearts of the town’s loyal pet owners. Desperate for an ally, Goldie turns to Cohen (Walker), the son of the former owner of the vet practice, for help. While they get off to a rough start, sparks start to fly as the two spend more time together, especially with Goldie taking over planning duties for the annual Christmas parade that will feature the four-legged and furry residents of the town this year.

It’s not just their characters who have love for each other, though. Both Cahill and Walker have a deep appreciation for each other and their decades-long friendship. In talking with Hallmark on set, both of these iconic stars shared how excited they were to be sharing the screen together for the first time. Take a look:

A post shared by Hallmark Channel (@hallmarkchannel)

It can be easy for the human actors to get upstaged by their animal co-stars, especially when there are so many different types of animals in a movie (cows, alpacas, and of course dogs in this case), but Cahill and Walker managed to hold things down even in the face of an adorable, overweight corgi. It’s a testament to the chemistry these two have on screen.

Their characters don’t share as much time on screen together as some of the other couples in Hallmark’s Christmas movies. However, the time they are together is swoonworthy — well, once they got over their meet-cute, that is. I definitely wouldn’t mind a sequel revisiting Goldie and Cohen a year from now. Or, better yet, I’d love to see Cahill and Walker star in even more Hallmark movies together now that it’s clear that they play compelling and entertaining romantic leads.

Blue Dog Valley might not be my favorite Hallmark Christmas movie of 2026, but it's still worth the watch. If you missed the live airing, you can stream it now with an active Hallmark+ subscription. While there, check out my favorite Cahill movie, Christmas on Cherry Lane, or my favorite Walker film, Three Wise Men and a Baby.

#3409. Eight Hacks Every Tidal User Should Know

I recently switched from Apple Music to Tidal, and I'm happy I made the change. The main reason is AI-made music: Tidal has stricter AI filtering than any other major streamer. The second reason is audio quality. While all major music streaming services do basically the same thing, Tidal's focus has always been on streaming music at the highest possible quality. While other streaming services have more or less "caught up" in terms of pure sonic fidelity, Tidal still is better at getting that quality to your speakers, if you know a few tricks.

If you're switching from Apple Music or Spotify to Tidal, you probably want to bring your playlists with you. Tidal points new users toward third-party transfer tools like TuneMyMusic and Soundizz. They both have a free tier, but they only transfers a few hundred songs gratis. My playlists are way bigger than that. The easy solution is to grumble and sign up for a month, then cancel when your tracks are transferred, but that didn't sit well with me. A playlist is just a collection of song names, so why should I have to pay anything to transfer it? To solve the problem, I came up with a simple script that transfers playlists from Apple Music and Spotify to Tidal. I will not be charging a fee. Here's how it works:

Download your playlist as a .txt file. You can do this directly from Apple Music under File>Library>Export Playlist. You can't from Spotify, but the free site Exportify will download any of your playlists as a spreadsheet file you can save.

Install Python on your system. Double click "install certificates" in the folder that opens after installation.

Download this script. Save it in the same file as your playlist.

Run the script: (For Mac, open Terminal. For Windows, go to the Command prompt. Type python3 on a Mac or py on Windows.) Drag the script into the terminal window and press enter. It should ask you to drag your downloaded playlist into the window next.

Sign in to Tidal. Hit "Approve" to give permission for Tidal to run the script.

Have a banana. The script is going to search for all the songs on your playlist and match them to Tidal's library, so it can take a little while. I tested it with a playlist from Apple Music with 2,397 songs. It took about 20 minutes and found 2,362 of my tracks, a 99% success rate.

Fix the leftovers: The program creates two separate text files for "orphans." One is songs it couldn't find and one is songs it might be worth double-checking manually.

If everything goes well, your large playlist should be available on Tidal.

Note: The script uses a community-created library to talk to Tidal, so it could stop working if Tidal changes things up.

Like most streaming services, Tidal has a "heart" button called "add to my collection." You can click on any track, album, or playlist to "like" and saved it. But Tidal also has a separate, somewhat mysterious "Save for Later" option that puts songs, albums, and playlists into a separate collection. There are a couple reasons for this. First, it keeps a running list of new-to-you music waiting for you on a rainy day, and secondly, it (presumably) affects your recommendation algorithm differently. While Tidal isn't open about every detail of its recommendation algorithm, I assume "save for later" has less weight (if any) on your future recommendations than "add to my collection."

On Tidal, tracks that are 100% AI-generated get an "AI" badge, earn no royalties, and are never placed on a Tidal-curated playlist. Users can flip a switch in Settings to either allow or disallow AI content, too. Simple, but there's a bit of nuance that goes beyond the on/off switch. You have to set the AI-toggle separately on each device you use Tidal on, even if it's the same account. I guess this is so I can listen to AI music in my car but not at my desk? Sadly, AI detection is not a science, so some AI-made, and partly AI-made, tracks may still get through.

If you're streaming music from a music app through Bluetooth, the output is automatically compressed to a lower quality, and your phone stays in charge, so a phone call or a notification can interrupt your music. But Tidal's Tidal Connect feature skips the middleman. Music streams directly from your wifi to your speaker and your phone becomes a remote control, so you can take a call, go for a walk, and even run out of phone battery and the music will keep playing.

Have an external device with Tidal Connect compatibility.

Make sure your speaker or other output device and phone or computer are on the same wifi network.

Click the icon again to switch back to your phone.

Plenty of wifi speakers don’t support Tidal Connect, so check before you buy. Tidal keeps the full list of supported devices on its site. There's everything there from WiiM Mini—a $99 small box that adds Tidal Connect to speakers you already own—to dCS components that cost more than a car.

Tidal Connect isn't the only way to get the highest quality audio from Tidal. You can go for an old school, wired path like I have. I play audio from my desktop and route it directly to a mixer via USB. Here's the set-up:

Settings > Streaming > Audio Quality: Max.

Sound Output: choose your mixer as the output device instead of your computer’s speakers.

Exclusive Mode: On. It’s under Sound Output > More Settings. Tidal sends audio straight to the mixer at each track’s native sample rate, without your computer resampling it or mixing in system sounds.

Force Volume. It's in the desktop app next to Exclusive Mode, under Settings > Streaming > Sound Output > More Settings. Force Volume means Tidal will always output at the highest volume. You'll be controlling the actual volume from your mixer.

To check what your mixer can handle, look at its maximum sample rate:

Mac: Open Audio MIDI Setup (in Applications > Utilities), click your mixer, and open the Format menu. The highest number listed is your ceiling.

Windows: Go to Settings > System > Sound, click your mixer, and look under Output settings > Format.

My cheap-ass mixer tops out a 16-bit/48kHz which is CD quality, but not Tidal's top of 24-bit/192kHz, but at least I can control the EQ. Speaking of...

It's much cooler to turn dials than mess with computer settings. Tidal doesn’t have an equalizer, so if you’re using Tidal Connect or a wired connection, you'll need something to shape the sound. Here are some options:

Your computer: System-wide EQ apps, like Equalizer APO on Windows or SoundSource on Mac, can adjust Tidal’s output. They don’t work with Tidal Connect though, which bypasses your computer’s audio processing.

Your speaker’s app: If you use a Tidal Connect speaker or streamer, it probably has a companion app for EQ.

A mixer or audio interface: Channel EQ knobs let you adjust bass, mids, and treble by hand, in real time.

Your speakers: Many powered speakers and studio monitors have low and high controls on the back.

A stereo receiver or amp: Old-school bass and treble knobs still work in 2026.

Most of Tidal's catalog streams as "better-than-CD quality" FLAC files at every subscription tier, so you might be inclined to click "play music at highest quality on everything." but settings are only as good as the gear you're using, and there are times when lower quality is the right choice. Here's when to turn down the settings:

When you're in your car: CarPlay and Bluetooth cut audio down to CD quality or less before it reaches your speaker, and with road noises, it usually doesn't matter anyway, so turn the streaming down to "High" instead of "Max." Or download your playlist before you leave, if you must have "as good as possible" audio.

You have a data cap and are off wifi. Top quality audio requires huge file transfer, so set your mobile data to High or Low and save Max for wifi.

Your connection is spotty: To avoid buffering, a lower setting keeps the music playing.

This isn't a universal hack, but some Android phones have microSD card slots, which can save you a lot of hassle if you're downloading a lot of audio files—an album at high quality might top 1GB, so having an external source will save you a ton of hassle. If your phone has a microSD card slot, go to Tidal's settings, find "download destination" and choose the memory card.

#3407. Decoding Kate Middleton’s “Tourdrobe” for Her Trip to India

When Kate Middleton stepped out on the green carpet at the Earthshot Awards ceremony in Mumbai this week, it was “an absolute princess moment,” says British designer Amanda Wakeley.

“Catherine has really come into her own. She has found her stride and a new confidence, and you see that in this dazzling but also practical ‘tourdrobe,’’’ Wakeley, who has previously dressed the Princess of Wales and used to dress Princess Diana, tells Vanity Fair.

It has been 10 years since Princess Kate last visited India. Her fashion choices are more sophisticated now than on her visit in 2016, and the speech she delivered at the Earthshot Prize ceremony on November 17 shows a new confidence. With her elevated look, there’s no trace of High Street labels. Kate’s flared floral dresses and the wedge shoes she used to love (but the late Queen Elizabeth apparently disliked) have been replaced by Manolo Blahnik pumps, couture power suits, and clothes by some of her favorite designers, such as Emilia Wickstead.

Prince William and Princess Kate attend The Earthshot Prize Awards Ceremony at the Jio World Convention Centre on November 17, 2026 in Mumbai, India.

Kate’s decision to wear a striking vermilion dress made from handwoven silk by New Delhi–based designer Mahima Mahajan to the Earthshot Prize ceremony spoke volumes. The eye-catching dress, which she paired with a burgundy Prada velvet clutch, was chosen after Kate had selected a special suite of emeralds from the royal gem collection. The green stones on the dress perfectly matched her jewels, which served as an homage to both Queen Elizabeth II and India, as the green of the Indian flag represents growth and prosperity.

The dazzling stones known as the “emerald tassel suite” were worn frequently by the late Queen Elizabeth II, and while Kate has previously worn the earrings, this marked the first time she wore the set. The effect was dramatic.

“Never has Catherine looked more like a queen in waiting,” Wakeley says of the look.

Wearing the suite ensured that Kate, who has free rein of the royal jewels, looked more regal than ever. “What was fascinating was seeing Catherine wear these incredible family heirlooms along with more relaxed collections from some of her favorite modern jewelry designers like Kiki McDonough and Astley Clarke,” remarks Wakeley.

Kate’s carefully curated wardrobe for the trip wasn’t just about power dressing—it was also about showing she can be sustainable as well as on trend.

“It was good to see Catherine making a proper nod to sustainability by rewearing her Roksanda dress,” Wakeley notes. “It’s clear a lot of thought has gone into her outfit choices. Her wardrobe has to be practical, and her clothes have to work harder than most people consider for their clothing; she needs weight in the hem of the floaty dresses. She has learned lessons the hard way. She is often seen bending down, talking to children, so she’s conscious of how low a neckline is, how short a skirt is.”

Princess Kate visits the Nowrosjee Wadia Maternity Hospital, on November 18, 2026 in Mumbai, India.

For her visit to Mumbai’s Nowrosjee Wadia Maternity Hospital on November 18, Catherine chose a striking red tailored Emilia Wickstead skirt suit with Manolo Blahnik pumps. On November 16, she opted for a pistachio blazer by designer Veronica Beard, paired with white Alexander McQueen trousers and pearl-buckled Camilla Elphick flats, a relaxed and accessible look for when she picked up a cricket bat.

Princess Kate plays cricket on November 16, 2026 in Mumbai, India.

As Princess of Wales, Catherine is often compared to Princess Diana. “The main difference is Diana was a fashion icon. Catherine has become a style icon,” Wakeley says. “There’s a big difference. Diana played into the fashion of the day and was finding her style. During the time she resigned from public life, she worked out her style DNA. Catherine has had to do that on the job. Very wisely, she has worked out her style and doesn’t get too impacted by fashion and trends. She goes for what she likes. What works for her rather than trends. She really knows now what works for her.”

#3406. A Doctor Doom And Doctor Strange Team-Up Is One Of The Best Marvel Comics Ever

Doctor Victor von Doom is a master of magic, so little surprise he's often crossed paths with the Sorcerer Supreme, Doctor Stephen Strange. Their first meeting, and the foundation for their mutual respect, was in 1989's "Doctor Strange and Doctor Doom: Triumph and Torment," one of the essential Doctor Doom comics every Marvel fan should read.

Written by Roger Stern, one of the best writers in the 1980s Marvel Comics bullpen, and drawn by Mike Mignola, future creator of the "Hellboy" universe, "Triumph and Torment" is indeed a triumph. It was published in the "Marvel Graphic Novel" line, itself designed to tell standalone and more mature stories featuring Marvel's character stable.

Doom's usual nemeses, Reed Richards and the Fantastic Four, are nowhere to be seen. While, conceptually, Doom needs Richards, tales like "Triumph and Torment" prove how he can hold individual stories without the FF. "Triumph and Torment" is also one of the most convincing arguments for Doom being more than a villain.

In Doom's debut, Stan Lee and Jack Kirby's "Fantastic Four" #5, it's established he had, during his and Reed's time at college, been obsessed with dark magic and built a machine to enter the nether world, which blew up and scarred him. His fuller origin in "Fantastic Four Annual" #2 revealed his ambition was to contact his mother, Cynthia von Doom, a witch who died during his childhood. Cynthia's trunk of magical secrets begat Victor's own knowledge of sorcery.

A 1971 story in "Astonishing Tales" #8 (by Gerry Conway and Gene Colan) then revealed that every Midsummer's Eve (when the liminal walls between worlds are the thinnest), Doom battles the forces of Hell to free his mother's soul, only to reach a stalemate. So, in "Triumph and Torment," Doom does the unthinkable and asks for help.

In "Triumph and Torment," both Strange and Doom partake in a contest of the world's greatest sorcerers held by Strange's god-like patrons, the Vishanti. Strange wins with Doom placing second — a familiar place for him, but it works in his favor. Per contest rules, Strange must grant a "boon" of Doom's choosing, and Doom wants Strange's assistance in freeing his mother's soul.

"Is one woman's soul beneath the notice of the Sorcerer Supreme?" Doom asks a surprised Strange, who in turns questions why Doom never requested his help before. "I will bear any ordeal, Strange, but Doctor Doom does not beg," he replies. That pride is ultimately crucial to Doom's plan to free Cynthia.

In Hell, facing the overwhelming power of the demon lord Mephisto, Doom seemingly trades Strange's soul for his mother's. But Cynthia, a noble woman, refuses and spurns Victor — a sacrifice that secures her place in Heaven. Doom finally frees his mother and outwits her devilish captor. This plan both flatters and damns Doom's character. He values his mother's safety more than her love for him, but his own pride most of all.

"Triumph and Torment" helps itself stand alone by exploring Doom and Strange's origins, so you can understand both men completely from this one story. Their journeys are also quite similar, as physical injuries prompt both men to venture high into the Himalayas seeking mystical knowledge. The book retells Cynthia's death, and Victor's childhood, via Doom's attendant Boris. Along with the reader, Strange realizes that beneath Doom's cold armor lies a child of tragedy. Upon taking his mask for the first time, Doom swears that pain and compassion are for lesser men — but his plan to free his mother, and what it costs him, prove otherwise.

Mike Mignola's art in "Triumph and Torment" makes Doctor Doom, his castle, and Latveria feel more truly gothic than in any other comic. Knowing Mignola went on to create a demonic superhero, too, it's hard not to compare "Triumph and Torment" to "Hellboy." Mignola drawing Strange and Doom facing down demons feels like a "Hellboy" test run in the same way his Batman comic "Sanctum" was.

In the documentary "Mike Mignola: Drawing Monsters," Mignola admitted he felt out of place drawing typical Marvel superhero books during the 1980s. "I'm not cut out to draw superheroes [...or] cars and buildings, most of the stuff that comics are made of," Mignola explained. He'd much rather be drawing monsters, which is why "Triumph and Torment" was a perfect assignment for him. Mignola's penciling especially comes to vibrant life once Doom and Strange enter Hell.

Far from looking identical, the demons all have different skin tones, weapons, and proportions. Some have wings, one is a humanoid torso on a giant serpent's tail, etc. Inker/colorist Mark Badger, rather than using a single background color for Hell, employs red-orange-yellow-green gradients. Mixed with Mignola's heavy shadows, it looks truly creepy, ethereal, and dangerous, like the typical fire and brimstone version of Hell but made even stranger. Compare this to the scary and lonely underworld in Mignola's 2010s series "Hellboy in Hell," and you can see an artist who grew.

Of course, the greatest achievement in "Triumph and Torment" is Doctor Doom's. In "Astonishing Tales" #8, Doom's goal to free his mother from eternal damnation is presented as a Sisyphean task he'll never achieve. Thinking he could break the laws of Hell is a sign of Doom's immense self-regard and ambition — and incredibly, he eventually did it.

#3403. Avengers: Doomsday Trailer Finally Gives Cyclops The X-Men Line Fans Were Waiting For

If you thought the wait to finally hear Chris Evans' Steve Rogers announce (well, more like theatrically whisper), "Avengers, assemble!" in 2019's "Avengers: Endgame" was long enough, then that's nothing compared to the plight of "X-Men" enthusiasts ever since the first 20th Century Fox film came out in 2000. Arguably no fanbase has suffered more in that time, enduring a steady stream of relatively comic book-y blockbusters that mostly just seemed embarrassed of their own source material, with only a few exceptions thrown into the mix. Whatever you might say about "Avengers: Doomsday" leading up to its release, however, "comic book-y" has to be at the top of the list — and the final "Doomsday" trailer has just given us the famous line every nerd has been dying to witness.

Yes, this is a perfect excuse to link to the memorable "Say the line, Bart!" gag from "The Simpsons." "X-Men" fans have read it in the comics, they've actually seen it before in the animated "X-Men: '97" series, and it basically seemed like a fait accompli that Marvel would find a way to deliver this moment in live action for "Doomsday." You know what we're talking about: Cyclops (James Marsden), leader of the mutant team of superheroes, finally bellowing out, "To me, my X-Men!"

The only wrinkle is probably the idea of dropping this reveal in a trailer, as opposed to saving it for the movie itself. Would it have been ideal to experience this for the very first time in theaters on opening weekend, rather than on your phone while walking into work on a Monday morning? Of course! Does that make the actual scene any less thrilling? Probably not! So, without further ado, let's overanalyze this to within an inch of its life below.

Could anyone have imagined seeing this comic book panel come to life before their very eyes in "Avengers: Doomsday"? Okay, sure, the circumstances aren't exactly what most fans would've anticipated in a vacuum. Rather than seeing this moment occur after several successful "X-Men" movies spent years carefully laying the foundation for Scott Summers to become the leader of the team we know and love from the comics, this is getting shoehorned into a crossover movie pitting a few familiar "X-Men" film stars against a villain they have no real connection to in Robert Downey Jr.'s Doctor Doom. And despite the "X-Men"-centric nature of this call to action, it's at least a little funny to hear him specifically assemble his fellow mutants and then watch several members of the Avengers and Fantastic Four arrive in perfect formation.

But between the awfully long wait for this moment and James Marsden's delivery of this dialogue (which is pretty similar to the one in Season 1 of the widely well-received "X-Men '97"), it's tough to imagine many fans out there will feel inclined to nitpick anything. Directors Joe and Anthony Russo are clearly hoping this begins to set things right for a group of mutants who've deserved a much better live-action fate than they've typically received. So, while the internet spends the next few weeks arguing over whether this sequence had the requisite amount of hype and payoff to decades of build up, the rest of the moviegoing population has probably already been convinced to fork over approximately $2 billion for this latest "Avengers" extravaganza. So it goes!

The Avengers, X-Men, Fantastic Four, and more will arrive in "Avengers: Doomsday" on December 18, 2026.

#3401. Google launches Gemini 4 Neon with Carbon quality at Flash speeds, live for AI Pro

Following last week’s release of Carbon and Hydrogen, Google today is rolling out Gemini 4 Neon. The model offers “frontier-level reasoning for complex, high-frequency workflows faster and more cost efficiently.”

Before today, Google’s Gemini 4 family consisted of:

Neon has performance comparable to, if not surpassing, Carbon across coding, reasoning, and agentic tasks, but at Flash speeds and a lower cost.

In the Gemini app, Google says to expect:

Honestly it's getting difficult to keep up with all these names 😩 It seems like they're taking the OpenAI / Anthropic approach on this.

I personally like the previous naming scheme with Flash and Pro. You could easily tell which one is more advanced and which is a "lighter" quicker model.

But on surface level when I look at the model selector in Antigravity, how am I supposed to know which model is better for my needs? Argon, Hydrogen, Carbon, or Neon????

Same with ChatGPT - Astra, Sol, Terra, and Luna

And Anthropic - Mythos, Fable, Opus, Sonnet and Haiku

Maybe I'm just getting old 🥵 but i wish I didn't need to research which models to use for my work and was way simpler.

Neon has the same 1 million-token context window with four thinking levels, like Hydrogen: Low, Medium, High, and Extra High. Officially, the new model sits between Hydrogen and Carbon in the Gemini 4 family.

Neon is built for complex coding, analytical reasoning, and production-grade enterprise workflows. While Carbon tackles your hardest, long-horizon projects and Hydrogen handles fast everyday execution, Neon balances depth and efficiency.

Neon is priced at $3/1M input tokens and $15/1M output tokens, or twice as expensive as Hydrogen. Argon and Carbon cost $2/1M input and $10/1M output until November 30. After the promotional pricing, it will be $4/1M input and $20/1M output, with Neon 25% cheaper as a result.

#3400. Cillian Murphy Regretted Not Being Part Of One Christopher Nolan Movie

Speaking to the Independent back in 2023, Cillian Murphy admitted there was one Christopher Nolan movie that he would've liked to have worked on but didn't. The film in question? Nolan's 2014 space odyssey "Interstellar."

Murphy has, to date, appeared in six of Nolan's movies. He played Dr. Jonathan Crane, aka the Scarecrow, in Nolan's three Batman movies (albeit, two of those performances were cameos), and he portrayed Robert Fischer, a man subjected to dream invasion, in "Inception." He also played a soldier in "Dunkirk" and won an Academy Award for Best Actor for portraying the titular character in Nolan's "Oppenheimer." And while he's great in all these roles, some of Murphy's performances in Nolan's films are even better than others.

As for "Interstellar," Murphy told the Independent that while he wishes he could've been involved with it, he loves it all the same, explaining:

"I adore 'Interstellar' just because I find it so emotional. [...] I remember seeing it in the cinema when I had little kids. It just had a big impact on me. It broke my heart. I love watching his films when I'm not in them because you don't have to freak out about the size of your ears, or whatever."

That said, Murphy clarified that the "right people" were ultimately cast in "Interstellar." Indeed, the film is full of big-name stars, including Matthew McConaughey, Anne Hathaway, Jessica Chastain, John Lithgow, Michael Caine, Ellen Burstyn, Casey Affleck, Topher Grace, David Oyelowo, and Matt Damon. Given the prestige of that cast, Murphy likely would've been happy to tag in for any of those actors.

Cillian Murphy was interviewed by the Independent right around the time "Oppenheimer" opened in theaters, and it was brought to his attention that many filmgoers had, amusingly, paired the movie with Greta Gerwig's "Barbie" to create a deliberately incongruous double-feature widely referred to as "Barbenheimer." It was quite the cultural event as well, with "Barbenheimer" going on to become a massive box office success.

Playfully, the Independent asked Murphy which Christopher Nolan film he would pair "Oppenheimer" with, and he presented the following options:

"You could go 'Interstellar,' which is very ... explores similar scientific, physic themes. Or you could watch 'Dunkirk,' which is also set in World War II. 'Dunkirk' is shorter, so that might be a good match 'cause it's like an hour-and-a-half, and then you can go into ['Oppenheimer']."

"Dunkirk" is, just for the record, 106 minutes, but I get Murphy's meaning. "Oppenheimer" is already three hours, and "Interstellar" is 169 minutes, so pairing two very long movies together might be a bit of a chore.

Nolan has since directed the 2026 mega-hit "The Odyssey," while, in the same year, Murphy made his long-awaited return to the "28" franchise by appearing briefly in "28 Years Later: The Bone Temple." One can assume, however, that Murphy and Nolan will cross paths again professionally in due time.

#3399. Eight Important Router Settings You Should Check (or Change)

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Your router is a key piece of your home network, as it connects all of your other devices to the internet. This also makes it a highly valuable target for attackers and can leave your data vulnerable—especially if you simply plug your router in with its default settings unchanged. Whether your router is brand new or it's been a while since you audited your existing setup, these are the key settings to check and change right now.

Your router's security protocol determines how encryption and authentication work to protect data that's transmitted over your network. WPA3 Personal is the newest standard and the most secure, so if it's available on your router, enable it. It's compatible with devices that support Wi-Fi 6. Some older devices may not work with WPA3, in which case the WPA2/WPA3 Transitional mixed mode is a good alternative. At minimum, set your router to WPA2 Personal (AES).

Some routers ship with factory default login credentials, which are the username and password you need to access your device's admin dashboard. (This is not the same as your network name or wifi password, which you set up later.) Default router passwords are searchable online, which leaves your router's admin settings open to anyone. Once you get into your dashboard for the first time, change the default credentials and enable two-factor authentication for your admin account if available.

While some newer routers do have unique, device-specific defaults, it's a good idea to check this setting and ensure it's secure. If you're prompted to create custom admin credentials during the setup process, do it.

Your network name, or SSID, is how your network appears when you search for available wifi. By default, this may be the name of the router brand or a short string of characters, but you should choose something unique to your network. Make sure there's no identifying personal information, such as your name or house number. While you may be tempted to hide your network and obscure your SSID, this may actually make your information less secure, so keep this setting disabled. You can, however, add "_nomap" to the end of your network name, which prevents your router's physical coordinates from being mapped by location databases.

The password to access your network should also be unique and secure and should not include obvious personal information. One option to keep it memorable and easy to type is to create a passphrase using five to seven unrelated words that, combined, have at least 16 characters.

Being able to log into your router's admin dashboard from anywhere may be useful if you have complex networking needs or troubleshooting issues that often have to be addressed when you're away from home, but it also leaves an entry point open for attackers. Turn off remote management to prevent anyone from accessing your dashboard unless they are on your network. (This is also a great reason to have strong, unique admin credentials.)

Two additional settings that leave your network vulnerable are Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS) and Universal Plug and Play (UPnP). The former lets users connect to your network with a PIN, which can be vulnerable to brute-force attacks. The latter allows smart devices to easily connect to your network—but this also allows malware to spread more readily. You may need to have UPnP on in order to connect devices initially but should disable it afterward.

Any easy win for your network security is segmenting traffic to different networks, so if one is compromised, the data on the others remain unaffected. Many wifi routers have a "guest mode," which creates a separate SSID and password that you can share with visitors instead of giving them your primary network credentials. You can also set up a separate network for all of your smart home and IoT devices so exploitable vulnerabilities in these devices don't put your computers, phones, and other connected devices at risk too.

Routers run a type of software—called firmware—just like any other device. Firmware controls the router's core functions and is not immune to vulnerabilities, which can be exploited by bad actors. And, just like other types of software, manufacturers occasionally push updates to patch these flaws. Check your router's dashboard to see if automatic updates are toggled on. Some devices require an opt-in for auto updates during setup, so you should enable them if they are off. Some routers may even require manual updates—in this case, set a monthly or quarterly (at minimum) calendar reminder to check for patches.

Warning! Spoilers ahead for Season 9, Episode 7 of FBI, “Posterity,” streaming now with a Paramount+ subscription.

Over the last few years, FBI has seen a surprising amount of cast changes in such a short amount of time. Just last season, the CBS procedural said goodbye to Emily Alabi not long after she joined the cast, and Juliana Aidén Martinez was then brought on. After a recent update on the procedural pointed towards another exit on the 2026 TV schedule, I had to ask one star all about it, and they totally get why I have questions.

Earlier in this season of FBI, John Boyd’s Stuart Scola revealed that wife and baby mama Nina Chase (Shantel VanSanten) had been offered the chance to lead her own task force in San Diego. Despite some hesitation, Scola ultimately tells her she should take it, and last week’s episode, “Posterity,” saw Nina getting ready for the big move. After some thinking, Scola told her he was going to put in a transfer to move to California with her, even if it would take a while.

That development led me, and likely many fans, to worry that another exit could be coming and that we might say goodbye to Scola in the near future. However, Boyd told CinemaBlend what’s really going on and sought to ease concerns:

I mean, look, as far as I know, there's no plans for any major changes, but I think that's a perfectly natural question to have. But really what's happening is exploring the character in a relationship in a very real way of something that we haven't yet tried with this couple, which real couples go through, all the time in life, which is career changes and geographics and movement. And what does it mean to love someone and let them go, ask them to stay, give up your thing?

Boyd's comments seem to point to the writers simply wanting to shake things up for Nina and Scola in a way they've never done before. The actor also told us this:

It's sacrifice and change, and it makes them super relatable. So, that's the story we're telling for now, but it's perfectly fine to kind of, hopefully, tease the idea of certain characters not being around anymore to see if people really love them.

I’m relieved to know that Boyd’s not going anywhere, at least not any time soon and that this is merely a chance to explore Scola and Nina’s relationship in a different way. When Nina was revealed to be moving to San Diego, there was no telling where things could be going for her and Scola, as well as their son, Dougie. And after the several cast exits the show has had in recent years, I appreciate the Boyd seems to understand why viewers would have questions.

Throughout the years, Nina and Scola have been through a lot, both as a couple and individually. While fans haven’t seen much of them since FBI: Most Wanted was canceled, we have been getting small updates here and there. Plus, VanSanten returned last season for the much-anticipated Scolina wedding. There's no telling how the relationship will progress, given they're working on opposite sides of the country and trying to raise their son together. I, for one, am eager to see how it plays out.

Also, even if there aren’t any plans to move Scola to San Diego in the near future, that isn’t stopping potential Scolina spinoff ideas. When asked by CinemaBlend if FBI could expand with another spinoff centered on Scola and Nina in San Diego, VanSanten said she was already campaigning for a new series. Unsurprisingly, Boyd reiterated his intention to stay with the Mothership. But, if we do eventually see Scola leaving 26 Fed, it would be fun to follow the fan-favorite couple in California.

I’m excited to see what FBI has planned for this next Scolina obstacle, and as long as Boyd is not leaving the series any time soon, I’ll be fine. All in all, fans should really stay tuned in as Season 9 continues. The show returns with a new episode on Monday, November 30, at 8 p.m. ET on CBS, streaming the next day on Paramount+.

Passionate writer. Obsessed with anything and everything entertainment, specifically movies and television. Can get easily attached to fictional characters.

#3397. Apple Card doubles Daily Cash rewards for new customers in limited-time offer

If you’ve been thinking about getting an Apple Card, now might be a good time. Users who apply for an Apple Card through December 10 are eligible to earn double Daily Cash for their first year. Here are the details.

As spotted by MacRumors, Apple is offering a limited-time promotion that doubles Daily Cash rewards for new Apple Card customers, which in practice means eligible users can earn up to 6% cash back on purchases during their first year.

If you’re not familiar with the Apple Card’s Daily Cash, Apple describes it as a “no points, no gimmicks” cash back program. Here’s how the company explains it:

Get Daily Cash back from a percentage of your purchases. Not a month from now. Every day. There’s no limit to how much you can get.

With the promo, which is available exclusively through this link, new Apple Card users will see these values double to 6% on purchases from Apple and select merchants using Apple Pay, 4% on purchases made with Apple Pay, and 2% on purchases made with the physical or virtual card.

Apple notes that there is a $1,000 limit on the additional Bonus Daily Cash earned through the promotion. Once that limit is reached, rewards return to the standard 1%, 2%, and 3% rates, even if the first year hasn’t ended. The usual “merchant offers may change at any time” disclaimer also applies to the higher cash back rates.

Still, this looks like a pretty compelling offer for anyone who was already considering applying for an Apple Card.

To learn more about the promotion and apply, follow this link.

#3396. Focker In-Law Review: Ben Stiller And Ariana Grande Bring New Laughs To An Old Franchise

There's an unwritten rule that says most comedy film franchises suffer from diminishing returns. In general, it's hard to dispute that claim, as even several solid examples of funny comedy sequels tend to lack the freshness and originality of their predecessors. Thanks to this phenomenon, the existence of good comedy sequels, and especially good comedy franchises, feels almost unheard of.

That said, the "Meet the Parents" franchise is one that has quietly yet persistently endured over the past 26 years. (Even longer than that, if you consider the fact that the 2000 film is in fact a remake of the hard-to-find 1992 original.) The initial film in the series, starring Ben Stiller as the hapless, unfortunately named Greg Focker, debuted early during the '00s "cringe comedy" trend, part of a wave of films and shows which delighted in the awkwardly relatable suffering of its protagonists. The family sitcom nature of the film helped lead to two more sequels, "Meet the Fockers" and "Little Fockers." The latter movie appeared to close out what was a trilogy for the last 16 years, until the release of "Focker In-Law" this month.

Given Hollywood's recent over-reliance on pre-existing IP, it wouldn't have been surprising to see such a movie be a lazy legacy sequel, milking the franchise for anything it had left (despite its lack of nipples). This is why the film is such a pleasant surprise, as it manages to recapture much of what made "Meet the Parents" hilarious without resorting to too many callback bits. Rather than merely flipping the first film's script and having the legacy cast pass the torch to younger characters, "Focker In-Law" impressively continues Greg's journey. Its a film whose cast and crew manage to find new laughs within an old franchise.

Being a legacy sequel, "Focker In-Law" naturally brings back as many of the characters seen throughout the prior movies as it can. In addition to Ben Stiller's Greg, his wife Pam (Teri Polo), her father Jack (Robert De Niro), his wife Dina (Blythe Danner), and even Pam's ex-fiancé Kevin (Owen Wilson) appear here. (Those hoping to see Greg's parents Bernie and Roz, played in the past by Barbara Streisand and Dustin Hoffman, are out of luck.)

Thanks to the 16 year gap between sequels, Greg and Pam's children Henry and Samantha have grown up, and are now played by Skyler Gisondo and Beanie Feldstein, respectively. The plot is "Meet the Parents" in reverse; where that film saw Greg attempt to ingratiate himself with Jack before marrying Pam, now Henry is bringing home a woman he's hoping to marry: Olivia Jones (Ariana Grande).

It would've been easy for writer/director John Hamburg (who devised the story along with Ilana Glazer and Austen Earl) to pull a "The Force Awakens" on "Meet the Parents" and follow either Henry as he attempts to convince his dad and grandfather about his fiancé, or Olivia as she tries to win them over herself. Instead, Hamburg smartly keeps the focus on Greg's empty nest anxieties, allowing the franchise to grow older with him rather than try to pivot to a younger generation. It's a savvy choice, particularly because it doesn't require anyone to fill Stiller's shoes. After all, Stiller has not only perfected this character but also the comedic tone of the films. "Focker In-Law" contains some gags that would easily be over the top in the hands of someone less experienced, but Stiller can make Greg foolish while being sympathetic enough so things never go too far.

There's no getting around the fact that "Focker In-Law" is a mainstream studio comedy sequel, and as such it does occasionally fall prey to some of the pitfalls of that genre. For one thing, it's not a particularly striking looking film. While that's on par with the rest of the franchise (which never seemed too interested in focusing on production design or cinematography), it's a shame that it mostly relies on a standardized aesthetic to be broadly appealing rather than going for something unique. The scourge of broadness does also crop up in some of the gags, including the moment where a series of mishaps causes Jack to be "baby birded" someone else's food at the dinner table, which is easily the most groan-worthy joke in the film.

That said, it's commendable that such a joke is the summit of the film's lowest common denominator, for the bulk of the set pieces are expertly constructed. A running joke about Jack's aggressive dog hating Greg escalates to a degree of chaos that's worthy of vintage John Hughes, something that's not easy to do given that writer's hugely influential status. In the same way John Hamburg could've given into temptation to make "Focker In-Law" a more conventional legacy sequel, he also could've fallen into the trap of making this sequel bigger and crazier.

Instead, his history with the franchise means he innately understands that the films' bread and butter lies in steady escalation rather than sharp left turns. Ben Stiller can be set on fire and then almost frozen alive later, but such stunts wouldn't work if they weren't deployed correctly. Hamburg and company know just how much and what type of track to lay for the train to reach the station.

The secret sauce of "Focker In-Law" is that it succeeds thanks to a thorough commitment to character. All the best comedy is character-based. While Ben Stiller's Greg is the film's centerpoint, the supporting characters are just as vital. Robert De Niro gives Jack a warmer demeanor this time around. Owen Wilson turns up Kevin's smarm to 11. Skyler Gisondo proves once again how deft a performer he can be, making Henry a comedic variant on his Decoy Dan from "Primetime," as he tries to be his own person while attempting to placate a father figure.

Ariana Grande has perhaps the hardest task in the movie, as her Olivia needs to walk the line between sweet girl next door and, in Greg's eyes, a master manipulator villainess. Her excellent performance allows the film to indulge in some broad tonal swings while keeping Olivia believable as a human rather than a caricature.

For folks whom "Meet the Parents" and its sequels were more excruciating experiences than hilarious comedies, "Focker In-Law" isn't going to change your mind. Yet for those of us who've related to Greg Focker's plight and foolish behavior over the years, the film is a little gift. It still has a broad relatability in its observations on family and relationships. Yet it's also refreshing in how it commits to following Greg on his never-ending journey to be a better person. Thanks to this commitment, "Focker In-Law" has given its franchise a new lease on laughs.

"Focker In-Law" is in theaters on November 25, 2026.

#3395. Prince William Reportedly Wants to Strip Prince Harry of His Titles

Prince William is reportedly actively considering a plan for a “far-reaching restructuring” of the British monarchy, which he would implement once he ascends to the throne. His brother, Prince Harry, would be at the forefront of these changes: The future monarch reportedly wants only active members of the royal family who carry out duties on his behalf to retain their royal titles and the style of “Royal Highness.” These titles would therefore no longer be an “automatic privilege of birth” but would instead be equivalent to a “job title.”

The plan was detailed by Tom Sykes, a journalist and writer specializing in the royals, in his book Dukes of Hazard, to be published next February, excerpts of which were published by the Mail on Sunday on Saturday, November 21. The author, “a royal authority with impeccable society contacts” as the newspaper puts it, is said to have obtained confessions from friends of Prince William.

“If you are a working royal—going out, touring the country, doing diplomatic work, doing government work, having a public role, pressing the flesh, getting out of bed on a wet Wednesday to go to Sheffield—then you will be an HRH and you will have a prince or princess title. You will also get an allowance, a salary, and a place to live. One place to live,” the associate of the prince explained to Sykes. “If you are not doing those things and you are not a working royal, you will not get to be an HRH, you will not get a free or subsidized place to live, and you will not get any special favors. You will, however, be a private citizen free to get on with your life and make money any way you choose.”

By implementing this measure, Prince William hopes to prevent potential media scandals regarding the legitimacy of certain individuals’ right to retain their titles if they are not prominent members of the Firm (Prince Harry) or if they are under legal scrutiny (Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor). But also, and above all, the Prince of Wales hopes to offer an option to his children, Princess Charlotte, 11, and Prince Louis, eight, who could easily renounce their titles to pursue independent careers. The question does not arise for the eldest child of the Prince and Princess of Wales, Prince George, 13, whose future as heir to the throne is “guaranteed.” In fact, none of the three use their royal titles, preferring simply to be called by their first names and the surname Wales.

Under the rules established by King George V in 1917, the title of prince or princess, along with the predicate, is granted at birth to the sovereign’s children and to the children of the sovereign’s sons, as well as to all the children of the Prince of Wales’s eldest son. Prince William’s children, therefore, received these titles at birth, while Prince Harry’s children, Archie and Lilibet (ages seven and five), did not become prince and princess until King Charles III ascended the throne.

They may have to give them up if Prince William carries out his plan. “Under William’s current plan, the prince and princess titles of Harry and Meghan’s children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet, would be legally removed, along with the royal styles and princely titles of Harry and Meghan themselves,” writes Tom Sykes in his book. To do so, according to Sykes’s book, constitutional advisers have told William that he could issue letters patent, an official document authorized by the king. Such a decision could strain the relationship between the two brothers.

Sykes is convinced that Prince William would garner the approval of his subjects and “enormous public support in a country increasingly impatient with the cost and perceived excess of a sprawling royal household,” according to those close to him.

In October 2025, Prince William confided to actor Eugene Levy—whom he was hosting at Windsor Castle for the taping of Levy’s show The Reluctant Traveler—that “there are points when you look at tradition and go, Is that still fit for purpose today? Is that still the right thing to do? Are we still doing and having the most impact we could be having?”

Kensington Palace, however, declined to comment on the rumor. “As a matter of policy, we don’t comment on books or claims made within them.”

Originally published in Vanity Fair France.

#3393. Prime Video's God Of War Series Is Bringing One Video Game Cast Member Into Live-Action

The upcoming "God of War" TV series is bringing back a very recognizable face from the smash-hit games that inspired it. In the latest significant bit of casting for the Prime Video adaptation, actor Deborah Ann Woll has been chosen to reprise her voice role as Faye (aka Laufey), the late wife of Kratos, who looms incredibly large throughout the events of both mainline games and the upcoming spin-off titled "God of War Laufey." The news comes straight from Sony Pictures Television and Amazon MGM Studios, with the official press release describing the character as:

"The mysterious late wife of Kratos and mother of Atreus, Faye's abrupt passing sets in motion the events of 'God of War.' Along their journey, Kratos and Atreus discover secrets about Faye that make them wonder how well they truly knew her at all."

As gamers know, Faye's death prior to the events of the 2018 "God of War" game — the first in the more modern-generation games that shifted the action to Norse mythology — essentially kicked off the journey of Kratos and his young son Atreus as they discover hidden threats, newfound allies, and a much wider world than either character ever could've imagined. The "Daredevil" star now joins a packed cast that includes Dave Bautista as Kratos (taking over for original star Ryan Hurst, who injured himself during filming), Callum Vinson as Atreus, Mandy Patinkin as Odin, Ólafur Darri Ólafsson as Thor, Alastair Duncan as Mimir, and plenty more.

Look, if you can't beat your pitch-perfect casting from the first time around, then you might as well bring them back again. Deborah Ann Woll lent her voice and facial model to the character of Faye, starting with the 2018 "God of War" game, continuing with the highly-acclaimed sequel "Ragnarök," and soon taking on the lead role (yes, despite the inconvenience of Faye's death) in 2027's "God of War Laufey." Now, she's set to suit up in live-action for the Prime Video series, which is set to run for two full seasons as our next major video game adaptation.

This is both a strong vote of confidence in Woll's abilities as a performer (who most recently reprised her role as Karen Page in "Daredevil: Born Again") and an acknowledgement that, for certain characters, the original voice actor was simply the perfect choice all along. It's incredibly easy to imagine her bringing the same amount of pathos, tragedy, and bittersweet moments amid various flashbacks and visions that Kratos experiences throughout the saga ... and, perhaps, even in some original scenes further fleshing out their strong dynamic in the show. After all, when you have someone as talented and capable as Woll to work with, you might as well make full use of her time.

Prime Video's "God of War" series comes from showrunner Ronald D. Moore, with "Shōgun" and "Fallout" director Frederick E.O. Toye helming the first two episodes of Season 1. After a brief pause following Ryan Hurst's injury and the subsequent recasting of Dave Bautista, the show is currently on track for a likely 2027 release. Stay tuned to /Film for more casting and production updates as they come in.

#3392. The iPhone Duo Is Getting Face Unlock

Apple dropped iOS 27.2.1 last week, patching a handful of security vulnerabilities and bugs—including two iMessage flaws that let people read messages they shouldn't. But while most of us are running this version (or should install it as soon as possible), others are running something different—iOS 27.3.

Apple is currently beta testing the third major update in the iOS 27 era, and anyone—developer and public tester alike—is free to install it at their leisure. With it, comes the return of the Health app, vertical Safari tabs, and Siri AI app actions, among other new features. But for users of Apple's first foldable, the iPhone Duo, iOS 27.3 brings two rather notable changes—both of which are for the better.

With the second iOS 27.3 developer beta, Apple is introducing face unlock for the iPhone Duo. The foldable famously ships with Touch ID, the first new iPhone since the third-gen iPhone SE to do so. While that isn't a problem per se, many of us are used to unlocking our iPhones with our faces. This update just lets new Duo owners keep up with that muscle memory.

Now, take note: This isn't Face ID. No software update can introduce new hardware, so the iPhone Duo still doesn't have the camera tech required to power Apple's Face ID system. As such, the Duo's face unlock is likely not as secure as Face ID on other iPhones. Perhaps that's why your iPhone Duo will require Touch ID for Apple Pay and passwords, or after 45 minutes of inactivity. This feature seems to be one of pure convenience: If you want to be able to unlock your Duo with your face (at least, some of the time), you can.

What's more, this isn't a default setting. If you're running the beta, or if you're reading this after iOS 27.3 drops, you can find the option in Settings > Touch ID & Passcode.

Apple made a big deal about the continuity involved with opening and closing the iPhone Duo. As you do, your content moves with you seamlessly—a very Apple thing to do. That said, you might expect folding the Duo to lock it, but it doesn't. You need to hit the side button to actually put the phone to sleep.

iOS 27.3 changes that. If you so choose, you can enable a setting to lock your Duo whenever you close it. That won't work for everyone, of course—some users may still want to move between modes without worrying about locking their Duos. But for those who would rather lock their devices whenever they fold them up, the new option is under Settings > Display & Brightness.

#3390. One Element Of Avengers: Doomsday Has Me Excited Above All Else

"Avengers: Doomsday" is going to be one of the biggest movies of the year, if not ever, that much is certain. But so far, the movie's marketing has been quite, well, underwhelming. We already had one "Avengers" film (well, two) that relied entirely on gathering lots of known Marvel Cinematic Universe characters on screen at the same time. To do that again feels less special, as exciting as it is to see Cyclops (James Marsden) leading the X-Men into battle here.

Indeed, the worst thing one can say about this film right now is that it looks exactly like what you would expect. It's massive, sure, but it doesn't feel surprising in any way. Marvel announcing Robert Downey Jr. as Doctor Doom in the movie felt desperate, too, as it was obviously the studio's way of trying to win back the fans who'd been disappointed by the MCU's post-"Avengers: Endgame" output. "Spider-Man: Brand New Day" aside, Marvel's no longer the reliable hit machine that it once was.

That being said, there is one notable reason to be excited about "Doomsday." No, not the X-Men (though their inclusion is certainly cool) or the return of Scarlet Witch (Elizabeth Olsen). Instead, it's the fact that "Doomsday" is technically a direct sequel to "Thunderbolts*," itself by far the best non-"Spider-Man" MCU movie since "Endgame." More specifically, it picks up where that film left off, with the titular team (also known as the West Chesapeake Valley Thunderbolts sponsored by Shane's Tire Company) now officially being known as the New Avengers.

Sure enough, the final "Doomsday" trailer features a few shots of the New Avengers amidst all the new footage of Chris Evans as Steve Rogers, and it's enough to finally get me hyped for this film.

For the most part, the visuals in the final "Avengers: Doomsday" trailer look horrendously muted and dull, save for a single brief shot of David Harbour's Alexei Shostakov dressed in a horrendous New Avengers tracksuit staring in awe as Shang-Chi (Simu Liu) arrives at Avengers Tower. Immediately, the image both brightens the trailer and reminds you that as serious as "Doomsday" may be (with the old Avengers looking more tired and beaten up than ever), the New Avengers bring a whole different vibe to the table. After all, they're silly, not great at teamwork, and don't consider themselves to be gods. Instead, they talk through their psychological issues and even hug it out like something out of "Neon Genesis Evangelion."

As the final trailer makes clear, "Doomsday" is all about different superhero groups coming together. You have the remnants of the original Avengers team, the X-Men, the Thunderbolts/New Avengers, and the Fantastic Four — plus the stragglers from various MCU titles that we collectively kind of forgot about. Each brings a different dynamic to the film, with the New Avengers specifically being a group of loser superheroes and criminals not unlike the Guardians of the Galaxy ... with the big difference being that the former have to save themselves before they can save anyone else. It's why "Thunderbolts*" makes for such an emotional gut punch, especially when its leads come together as a team, and the idea of seeing them interact with the MCU at large does more to make "Doomsday" feel interesting than any number of cameos could.

"Avengers: Doomsday" will see the New Avengers suit up alongside their companions when it hits theaters on December 18, 2026.

TCL makes one of the best QLEDs for the money, and their technology keeps getting better. This TV supports Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos, and if you're a gamer, you get a refresh rate of 240Hz that is automatically triggered with its Auto Game Mode feature.

Gaming monitors can get pricey fast. At $159.99 (originally $299.99 at launch), this 27-inch Samsung Odyssey G55C curved gaming monitor offers a 1440p resolution, a 1000R curve, a 165Hz refresh rate with FreeSync and G-SYNC compatibility to keep screen tearing to a minimum, and features like Samsung’s Virtual Aim Point and Contrast Enhancer. It's a solid choice for gaming, especially at this price point.

Alienware makes great gaming laptops, and the Aurora is a great option for anyone who wants to get all the essentials without spending too much. At its current $1,099 price (originally $1,999), the Alienware Aurora 16 becomes a mid-tier gaming laptop at a "budget" price. We reviewed the higher-tier Aurora 16X and were impressed with it. The Aurora 16 has a slightly slower processor, a dimmer display with half the refresh rate, a smaller battery, and a weaker graphics card, but given its price, it's great for a gamer looking for a solid gaming laptop in the $1,000 range.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Yes. Walmart, Best Buy, Target, and Home Depot will all have in-store deals, some of which you might not find online, so if you're able to take a trip to your local retailer, keep your eyes open for different deals.

Amazon has a much larger inventory of tech products on sale, but the ones they both sell are mostly priced the same. While Amazon may have more deals, Walmart usually has a couple of surprise flagship tech products on sale that Amazon will later price match. So taking all of that into consideration, the best one will be whichever has whatever you're looking to buy at the lower price.

Yes. I own these headphones and can vouch they are worth every penny. The headphones are high quality and bring a hybrid style of open earbuds and bone conduction that I haven't seen in other headphones.

Disneyland live entertainment is few and far between as of late, which is a shame considering the Anaheim theme park used to boast some of the best shows. On November 21st, one of the last and most beloved nighttime shows, Fantasmic, went up in flames for the second time in three short years. With two incidents and Disney’s desire to cut back on live entertainment, I’m really starting to worry about the future of the show.

The fire reportedly broke out during Fantasmic’s second performance of the night shortly before the show’s finale. While the Mark Twain finale was able to go on, flames can be seen behind the boat on the small stage set up on Tom Saywer Island. Guests at the park were quick to pull out their phones and film the growing flames as the Mark Twain, full of classic Disney characters, made its way around the river. Take a look:

Here’s the Mark Twain Riverboat running during Fantasmic last night with the fire behind it. This happened during the 10:30PM show https://t.co/bMcOZ6z0PtNovember 22, 2026

The last two minutes of the show were canceled, and guests were asked to vacate the viewing area while the fire department handled the blaze. Thankfully, the fire was small compared to the 2023 incident that turned the Maleficent dragon animatronic into a giant fireball and forever changed the show. There’s been no word on the extent of the damage this time around, but considering the show was back Sunday night it safe to assume that nothing was affected and no cast members were harmed, thankfully.

Two fiery incidents are definitely a cause for concern, and with Disneyland executives’ history of scaling back entertainment to cut costs, I can’t help but worry about the show’s fate. After all, Fantasmic boasts a large cast of incredible performers and several floating units. Plus water screens, projectors, and fireworks. I’m no expert, but I’m willing to bet it’s one of the most costly attractions at Disneyland. Not to mention, the show is still feeling the loss of the Maleficent Dragon, which makes the battle between Mickey and Maleficent lackluster.

While I don’t think Disneyland would end the show without also announcing a replacement, I do think Disney fans should prepare themselves. After all, Disney fans aren’t known for taking new changes well. Just look at the uproar that happened when it was announced Dinosaur would close to make room for a new Indiana Jones attraction at Disney World.

Disneyland has been having a rough go at things this month. On the first day of the holiday season, the Anaheim theme park’s iconic fake snow was accidentally turned on during a rainstorm, creating a mess. Back in October, Frontierland experienced widespread flooding. With park tickets being so expensive, it’s unfortunate to see cracks in Disneyland’s magic, but not even the mouse can control the weather or unexpected fires.

#3387. Steven Spielberg's Next Movie Is A Star-Studded Western Written By Another Legendary Filmmaker

Earlier this year, Steven Spielberg announced that his next movie as a director would be a Western. This will be his first official crack at the most American of film genres, and that's reason enough for cinephiles to get excited.

Now, Deadline has revealed that the movie, an adaptation of Kevin Barry's novel "The Heart in Winter," will star Cillian Murphy, Jessie Buckley and Mark Rylance, and it's hard not to be elated. Factor in that Barry's book is being adapted into a script by Oscar-winner Paul Thomas Anderson, and there isn't a word in the English language to capture the utter exhilaration movie fans are feeling at this moment.

No one's more enthused than Spielberg, though. As he told Deadline:

"It's really the excitement for me to get to work together with my dear friend and colleague Paul Thomas Anderson on a genre, but more particularly, the genre notwithstanding, a story that quite quickly became close to both our hearts and we felt that we could do as a team."

Murphy will play Tom Rourke, an Irish immigrant eking out a living in Butte, Montana. He works as an assistant to a photographer and supplements his income by penning letters for illiterate miners seeking potential brides from the east. He needs the extra scratch, too, due to his alcohol and opium addictions. Tom is spiritually adrift until mail-order bride Polly Gillespie arrives in Butte. They fall fast in love, steal some money, and set what proves to be an eventful course for San Francisco.

Overall, Barry's book has echoes of Spielberg's theatrical directing debut on "The Sugarland Express," as it's about two lovers on the run from the law. But this being the late 1800s, and the pair being challenged as horseback riders, their journey isn't quite as fast-paced.

Kevin Barry's "The Heart in Winter" has been described as "a tragedy written as farce" (per The Guardian). Critics found it hilarious and wildly entertaining, and after his excellent work on "One Battle After Another," I can't imagine anyone more suited to a tale about a character with an opium addiction stealing a mail-order bride and heading to San Francisco than Paul Thomas Anderson. But what's most interesting to me is that this will be the first time Anderson has written an entire script for another filmmaker. He previously did rewrites on the Apple-backed "Killers of the Flower Moon" and "Napoleon" for Martin Scorsese and Ridley Scott, but he's the primary writer here.

As for Steven Spielberg, no filmmaker alive knows more about Western conventions than him, and you can rest assured he will aggressively avoid cliché. I mean, he'll be sure to keep the horizon line out of the middle of the frame, lest John Ford's eye-patched ghost haunt him for the rest of his days, but don't expect traditional Western violence of the shootout and saloon brawl variety. I haven't read the book yet, so I don't know if such scenes exist in Barry's novel, but if they do, they'll look unlike any shootout or brawl you've ever seen.

What's curious is that Spielberg went with the Montana-set "The Heart in Winter," given that he'd been talking about making a Texas Western. Texas is not Montana by a long shot, which makes me wonder if he might change the location of Barry's novel. I doubt he'd do that, so now he's cheesed off everyone in Texas who was hoping he'd make their state look sensationally epic. He'll have to make it up to them somehow.

#3386. Steven Spielberg Officially Takes On a New Genre for Next Movie

Cillian Murphy and Jessie Buckley are heading to the Wild West in a new film from the legendary director

Steven Spielberg is finally getting his chance to make a Western, and he's bringing some serious star power along for the ride. The legendary filmmaker is developing an adaptation of The Heart in Winter, with Jessie Buckley (Hamnet), Cillian Murphy (Oppenheimer), and Mark Rylance (Bridge of Spies) set to star.

As reported by Deadline, Spielberg will direct the movie for Focus Features, with an adapted screenplay by Paul Thomas Anderson (One Battle After Another). The project is based on Kevin Barry's novel of the same name and is expected to arrive in theaters sometime in 2028.

The story follows two star-crossed fugitives trying to find a place for themselves in the American West during the late 19th century. Spielberg and Anderson will also produce alongside Kristie Macosko Krieger and Sara Murphy.

Spielberg has spoken about wanting to direct a Western for years, and the opportunity to collaborate with Anderson was a major draw. Speaking to Deadline, the director said the story quickly became close to both filmmakers' hearts, making it a project they wanted to tackle together.

The collaboration is particularly notable because Anderson is writing the screenplay without directing the film himself for the first time. The filmmaker recently won an Oscar for Best Adapted Screenplay for One Battle After Another, making him an especially intriguing choice to bring Barry's novel to the screen.

Spielberg also revealed that Buckley and Murphy were his first choices for the two central roles, saying they were the only actors he could imagine playing the characters. The pair have never appeared in a film together before.

Production is expected to begin in the winter of 2027, according to Deadline. Spielberg also made clear that the Western isn't intended to be his final film, joking that if he wanted to ride off into the sunset, he would have made Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade his final movie.
