#3385. Siri Modular Apple Watch face gains two new styles with watchOS 27.3

Siri Modular, the new Apple Watch face in watchOS 27, is gaining new style options. watchOS 27.3, currently in beta, adds two more style options to the existing set. This gives users five options for adjusting what type of information appears on Siri Modular.

Siri Modular originally shipped with three style options. Each supports a small line complication above the time.

Additionally, the original three styles include these options:

In watchOS 27.3, Apple introduces two new Siri features that work with Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4.

First, there’s Siri Recap which uses the Apple Watch to turn audio into high-level text summaries. Second, there’s Live Rewind which lets you view a transcript of the last 15 seconds of spoken word.

The two new Siri Modular Apple Watch face styles help surface three things: invoking Siri, viewing conversations with Siri, and viewing Siri Recaps on the Apple Watch.

The new styles include a pill-shaped module that includes icon shortcuts that go directly to Siri conversations, invoke Siri AI, or go directly to Siri Recaps in the Siri app.

One style features a large digital clock with the new three-button Siri module. Another includes a compact digital clock with a Smart Stack tile and the new three-button Siri module.

This brings the style options to five. If you use the three circular complications configuration, you can also assign a Siri icon that invokes Siri AI.

watchOS 27.3 is currently in beta and expected to be released officially in December.

#3384. 5 Reasons Why The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping Ruled The Box Office

The biggest YA franchise in the game is back on top. Lionsgate released "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" in theaters over the weekend, and to say that the franchise's latest prequel film did well would be an understatement. This movie is already a huge hit for the studio and has brought the property back to its former, $100 million-plus opening weekend glory.

Directed once again by franchise shepherd Franchise Lawrence, "Sunrise on the Reaping" opened to a massive $120 million domestically. Internationally, the prequel bowed to $105 million, giving it a gigantic $225 million global start. It's now Lionsgate's biggest opening of 2026 overall. "Michael" ruled the box office with a $218 million global opening earlier this year, but "Sunrise on the Reaping" even managed to best the King of Pop. Now, whether or not this movie gets to the $1 billion mark like "Michael" in the long run is another question entirely, but it illustrates just how big this opening was.

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" looked like it was going to be a bigger hit than people realized, which proved true. It arrived right in line with bullish estimates, which climbed through the roof in the weeks leading up to its arrival. As such, it's now poised to become one of the biggest hits of the year overall.

So, what went right here? How did Lionsgate manage to make such a big bet and have it pay off so spectacularly well? We're going to look at the biggest reasons why "Sunrise on the Reaping" ruled the box office on its opening weekend. Let's get into it.

The biggest thing that this movie had going for it is that it wasn't just another "Hunger Games" film or a prequel for the sake of a prequel. It was a story that hardcore fans of the franchise have been waiting a long time to see. Specifically, one involving the famed games where Haymitch Abernathy, the character played by Woody Harrelson in the previous "Hunger Games" movies, won.

"Sunrise on the Reaping" pits a young Haymitch (Joseph Zada) against President Snow (Ralph Fiennes), to put it in the simplest possible terms. "Hunger Games" author Suzanne Collins wrote the book the movie is based on and, rather crucially, the novel was received very well by fans. And by most accounts, Francis Lawrence, with the help of Collins, delivered one heck of an adaptation. All of this to say, the movie promised something fans had been wanting for a hot minute and delivered the goods when the time arrived.

Beyond that, Jennifer Lawrence also broke her silence on her "Hunger Games" return in "Sunrise on the Reaping" ahead of the film's release, assuring that this movie was getting the original gang back together. That undoubtedly helped get more casual viewers on board who perhaps were only more interested in the original set of "Hunger Games" films. Overall, Lionsgate made the most of what this story had to offer, turning it into not just another movie but a true event within one of the biggest franchises of the last 20 years — one that demanded to be seen on the biggest screen available as soon as possible.

This is the kind of movie that hardcore fans were always going to be in the bag for, no matter what. That having been said, positive word of mouth never hurts. And while critics were, more or less, on this film's side, it worked like gangbusters for the intended audience. In the case of a long-running, beloved franchise, that is always more important.

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" holds a decent 69% critical approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes, as of this writing. However, it carries a stellar 94% audience score, which is near-universal praise from actual ticket buying fans. It also earned a damn good A- CinemaScore, which means word of mouth is going to be great in the weeks to come. Even though "Focker In-Law" could be a rare comedy box office hit over Thanksgiving, with Disney's "Hexed" opening as well, there should be more than enough room for this prequel to have a stellar second frame over the holiday weekend.

/Film's Nina Starner wrote that "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is a prequel that "delivers" in her review. Certain critics may have been a bit softer on it, but enough of them liked it to prevent the needle from being pushed down. More importantly, fans are loudly proclaiming their love for this film, which is going to do way more to motivate viewers who might have been on the fence to check it out in the coming weeks.

Lionsgate doesn't always have a lot of success when playing in the big-budget realm, but this franchise has generally been the exception to that rule. All of "The Hunger Games" movies have been hits at the box office and, save for the very first film, they've all benefited from November releases. This ended up being an "if it ain't broke, don't fix it" situation. All the same, the studio wisely picked the perfect spot on the calendar for this prequel to thrive.

Word of mouth can't be predicted, but getting in on an otherwise fairly dead pre-Thanksgiving weekend was very wise. "Sunrise on the Reaping" got one totally unimpeded weekend to do its thing and will now benefit from a long, five-day holiday weekend over Thanksgiving. It's basically going to have nine full days of ruling the box office before taking any sort of meaningful hit.

"The Hunger Games: Mockingjay — Part 2" ruled the box office in 2015, also in November, delivering a $102 million opening weekend en route to $653 million worldwide. This latest prequel had an even bigger opening, meaning it could eclipse that global figure when all's said and done. Not to get too ahead of ourselves, but it may wind up closer to "Mockingjay — Part 1" ($766 million worldwide), if all goes well.

Wherever the chips fall at the end of the day, it's going to be in large part because this movie wasn't competing with a slew of other blockbusters in the midst of a crowded summer. This is the big cinematic event of choice right now and will be for at least a couple of weeks.

It certainly doesn't happen too often, but if a franchise gets it right, the breakout sequel effect can come into play. One of the best examples in history is "The Dark Knight." While Christopher Nolan's "Batman Begins" was actually a bit of a box office disappointment, pulling in a so-so $373 million worldwide, "The Dark Knight" was simply too good to be ignored and made $1 billion at a time when movies rarely ever hit that milestone.

Other examples include "John Wick"/"John Wick: Chapter 2" and "Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse/"Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse." A very good first movie happened, people caught up with it after the fact, and that resulted in a much larger audience for the sequel. That brings us back to "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping." Despite being the sixth entry in this property, it benefited like a breakout sequel would have.

2023's "The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes" was a surprise victor at the Thanksgiving box office, ultimately pulling in nearly $350 million worldwide on a $100 million budget. A solid result, but it wasn't nearly what the first four movies in the "Hunger Games" franchise made. However, audiences and fans caught up with it and ended up enjoying it. So, after an eight-year break, Lionsgate kind of used that first prequel to prime the pumps on this franchise, even if that wasn't the intention.

The end result is that "Songbirds & Snakes" teed up the ball for "Sunrise on the Reaping," paving the way for the film to enjoy a much, much bigger opening than its predecessor. It's not a traditional breakout sequel, but it's a breakout sequel to a prequel people enjoyed.

Perhaps the most important factor when it comes to playing Monday morning quarterback with the success of "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" has to do with how big franchises are typically handled in Hollywood these days. Spin-offs. TV shows. Animated entries. Theme parks. More merchandise than anyone knows what to do with.

That never really happened with "The Hunger Games." That's in no small part because author Suzanne Collins has a lot of say over how those affairs are handled. Even so, there was an eight-year gap between movies by the time "The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes" came around and another three years before "Sunrise on the Reaping." Neither Lionsgate nor Collins ever allowed for overexposure to get the best of this franchise. That allowed for people to be legitimately excited about this film.

Former Disney CEO Bob Iger even admitted that multiple Marvel shows and Pixar movies going to streaming hurt those brands. The Marvel Cinematic Universe is mighty, but even fans grew tired of that. Likewise, Pixar is as good as cinema gets, yet audiences learned that they could just watch those movies at home. Meanwhile, Lionsgate has maintained discipline with the "Hunger Games" films and ensured that they remained cinematic events. Short-term gains and overdoing it would have potentially kneecapped what is now one of the studio's biggest hits in years. Hollywood could stand to learn a thing or two from this sort of execution.

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is in theaters now.

#3383. A Number of Banks Are Experiencing Outages Right Now

If you're having trouble accessing your bank right now, you aren't alone. As of Monday afternoon, a number of banks are experiencing outages and interruptions to service.

That's according to Downdetector, which collects user reports of issues to different sites and services. As of this article, the site shows notable numbers of user reports with the following banks and credit companies: American Express, Ally, Bank of America, Capital One, Chase, Citi, Huntington Bank, JP Morgan, Navy Federal Credit Union, USAA, US Bank, and TD Bank, Visa, Wells Fargo. Even PayPal, Venmo, and Zelle, money-transferring services, are showing user reports as well.

There isn't a clear reason why these various companies are currently experiencing issues. The timing is suspicious, of course: These interruptions come after last week's massive Microsoft outage, which took down services like Outlook, Teams, and Microsoft 365. It also comes just days after the FAA unexpectedly grounded all flights in the U.S. There's no evidence there's any link between these events, but the frequency of these developments is concerning on the surface.

For six seasons now, Abbott Elementary fans have faithfully watched the relationship between Janine Teagues (Quinta Brunson) and Gregory Eddie (Tyler James Williams) progress. The pair have gone from good friends to committed lovers over the past several years and, now, it seems we’re on the cusp of a proposal. Many viewers are hoping an engagement will come during the Disneyland-set 100th episode that’ll air amid the 2026 TV schedule. I’d love that as well, but I also have a question about two other characters.

Gregory and Janine are, of course, the core couple on Abbott, but plenty of other romantic relationships amongst characters have been highlighted as well. As we anticipate what lies ahead for Janine and Gregory, I can’t help but wonder what the future holds for Ava Coleman and O’Shon, who’ve been dating since Season 4. I’ve enjoyed seeing their relationship develop as well as the funny moments that have resulted from that. With that, it’s hard not to wonder what the long-term plan for them might look like.

It’s clear that the affable O’Shon (Matthew Law) and Abbott’s diva of a principal Ava (Critics Choice winner Janelle James) are on steady footing after some initial growing pains. At this point, the pair have not only vacationed together, but they’ve also reached the point where they can throw a party as a couple. (That Halloween shindig they held this season was fantastic). Some may think it’s a bit early to consider a proposal for these two, but I don’t think it’s wild to think it could happen by the end of Season 6.

Gregory first expressed interest in proposing to Janine at the end of Season 5, which was about two years after the two finally got together. Ava and O’Shon will be reaching that mark later in the sixth season and, while great TV couples have different timelines, I could see O’Shon popping the question soon. Plus, given how encouraging O’Shon has been amid Gregory’s attempts to propose, who’s to say the former doesn’t want that for himself sometime in the near future?

Of course, I’m not saying anyone needs to be jumping the broom by the end of this season. I just wouldn’t mind seeing one or two engagements by the time Abbott’s finale rolls around next spring. That may seem like a long shot for Ava and O’Shon right now, but I’m feeling very good about Janine and Gregory’s chances of hitting that milestone.

The True Story That Inspired Abbott Elementary’s Choice To Move The School Into A Mall

Gregory has been trying to orchestrate the right moment to present Janine with a ring. During the show’s latest episode, “Competition,” he attempted to land a reservation at a popular Italian restaurant, where he could propose. Ironically, that plan became moot once Abbott’s Step Team punched their ticket to Disneyland, and Janine informed her man that they’d serve as chaperones on the trip. So it now seems like a given that Gregory will attempt to propose while he and his lady are in “The Happiest Place On Earth.”

What’s more is that the pressure is going to be on, as Janine is aware of her beau’s intention to pop the question (thanks to a major slip-up on Ava’s part). So the pressure is really on for Eddie to craft the perfect proposal. The Disneyland episode could indeed present him the right situation to do just that and, if Gregory does pull it off in great fashion, it might set a bit of a bar for O’Shon to clear if he eventually takes that step.

We’ll just have to wait and see how it plays out when Abbott Elementary airs its hundredth episode on Wednesday, December 2 at 8:30 p.m. ET on ABC. Fans can also stream the show the next day with a Hulu subscription.

#3380. Avengers: Doomsday Final Trailer Breakdown - 5 Biggest Reveals And What They Mean

The new "Avengers: Doomsday" trailer shows MCU heroes assembling for their biggest battle yet. It will also surely be one of their most profitable, given the hype around this movie. Despite Marvel Studios' well-publicized troubles of late, the Avengers' return remains highly anticipated. As such, any new revelations Marvel is willing to provide about the team-up movie are significant to say the least.

The final "Doomsday" trailer doesn't actually feature any major reveals, which is a good thing for those who prefer to keep their theater experience as pure as possible. For those who like to know as much as they can ahead of a Marvel Cinematic Universe release, however, it means much of the movie remains a mystery. (We're still no clearer on whether Robert Downey Jr.'s Doctor Doom is actually a Tony Stark variant or not, despite Marvel Studios head Kevin Feige's recent comments.) That said, the latest tease did contain several notable moments that have only served to increase the already significant hype.

The new "Doomsday" trailer finally gives Cyclops the X-Men line fans were waiting for, when Marsden's hero delivers his "To me, my X-Men" rallying cry to assemble his mutants, the Avengers, Fantastic Four, and several other heroes. But beyond that tantalizing glimpse at the film's big showdown, there are several other notable moments, and lucky for you, we've gone and rounded 'em up.

The precise plot of "Avengers: Doomsday" remains under wraps for now, but at this point, we can pretty much piece together the major beats. Previously, co-director Joe Russo told Empire that Robert Downey Jr.'s Victor Von Doom is a "father who's a victim of trauma" and that he "lost a child." That lined up with what we've seen in previous trailers, wherein Vanessa Kirby's Sue Storm/Invisible Woman talked about how Doom "used to be different" before "everything he loved was taken from him." Now, the latest "Doomsday" trailer has confirmed that the Avengers themselves are responsible for it all.

In the new trailer, Chris Evans' Steve Rogers can be heard saying, "Years ago, we did what was needed to make the world right," in reference to the events of 2019's "Avengers: Endgame." He continues: "But we didn't know those choices would have consequences." It seems that Steve's choice to travel back through time to be with his lover, Peggy Carter (Hayley Atwell) — and whatever the Avengers did to defeat Josh Brolin's Thanos — caused some sort of multiversal upheaval in which Doom's daughter met her, well, doom.

This is why RDJ's villain tells the heroes of "Doomsday" that they've been living "stolen lives." With Steve's speech in the new trailer, it's all but certain he and the Avengers are responsible for whatever killed Doom's daughter, and likely the multiversal collapse referenced in the "Avengers Endgame: Encore" TVA scene. Turns out, Doom is the "consequence" to which Steve refers.

Thanks to what seemed like a hasty casting announcement prior to the final "Avengers: Doomsday" trailer, we knew Hailee Steinfeld's Kate Bishop would be appearing in the movie. Now, the trailer has given us our first look at the heir to the Hawkeye mantle in a very quick shot that shows her looking up at something that's clearly got her very worried. But Kate might be just one of the Young Avengers to appear in the film.

We know Scott Lang's (Paul Rudd) daughter, Cassie Lang (Kathryn Newton), is also part of "Doomsday." She shows up briefly in the new trailer, too, looking as concerned as Kate. Interestingly enough, both characters are in their superhero suits, which suggests they'll be joining the big fight against Doctor Doom. That means two members of the Young Avengers will be involved in "Doomsday." Marvel Studios has yet to officially introduce these heroes as the superhero group from the comics, but has been slowly building up this new generation of Avengers over the past few years.

The only likely member of the Young Avengers who hasn't appeared in trailers and is yet to be confirmed as being involved with "Doomsday" is Iman Vellani's Ms. Marvel. According to Andy Serkis, Ms. Marvel will appear in "Doomsday," but Marvel hasn't made that official. Otherwise, there are a handful of other young heroes that could show up and potentially form the Young Avengers proper in the movie itself, including Riri Williams/Ironheart (Dominique Thorne) and America Chavez (Xochitl Gomez). For now, it looks more likely than ever we'll see an official Young Avengers group unite in "Doomsday."

The new "Avengers: Doomsday" trailer shows Chris Hemsworth's Thor rising from the floor surrounded by yellow lightning as opposed to his typical blue lightning. That's significant, as it all but confirms he'll be wielding a powerful new force known as the Odinforce. This power, created by the Kings of Asgard, is a major upgrade for the character, and the latest trailer appears to have shown it in action.

One of the most frequently showcased "Doomsday" scenes thus far has been the moment in which Thor launches himself at Doctor Doom, only to be stopped mid-air and flung backwards by the villain's formidable force (which, as it happens, involves a Jacky Kirby-inspired energy blast from Doom). Clearly, the God of Thunder is as outmatched as the rest of his cohorts.

But back when the first four teaser trailers for "Doomsday" dropped, we saw Hemsworth's hero begging his father for the "strength of the All-Fathers." Since then we've seen concept art and a "Doomsday" billboard that seemingly spoiled the fact Thor was getting a major upgrade in the form of the Odinforce. It's this force that turns his lightning yellow, and the final "Doomsday" trailer is the first time we see footage of it in action. The brief shot shows Thor ascending in a forest, which looks to be the same forest in which he begged for the strength of the All-Fathers in the original teaser. Looks like he got his wish. Whether it will prove effective against Doom, however, remains to be seen.

We got our first look at the X-Men in "Avengers: Doomsday" courtesy of the X-Men-heavy trailer back in January 2026. Since then, we've learned how the mutants might find their way to the Avengers. The film will take place during the collapse of the multiverse, whereby several "incursions" will see planets and timelines collide. These collisions are likely to be the reason for the film's major crossovers, i.e. the Fox-era X-Men and the Fantastic Four arriving on the Avengers' Earth 616. But it seems when the X-Men and Avengers first come face to face they initially clash, as evidenced by footage from prior trailers in which Yelena Belova/Black Widow (Florence Pugh) takes on Mystique (Rebecca Romijn) and Shang-Chi (Simu Liu) battles Gambit (Channing Tatum).

Now, however, the final "Doomsday" trailer has confirmed that Anthony Mackie's Sam Wilson/Captain America will face off against James Marsden's Scott Summers/Cyclops. The trailer shows the pair going toe-to-toe in what looks to be a pretty brutal clash, with Wilson holding Cyclops by the neck as he unleashes an optic blast. Clearly, the X-Men and Avengers ultimately manage to, as Thor puts it, "put aside their petty squabbles." But for at least a moment, the two superhero teams will be at odds in the movie, and Sam Wilson's showdown with Scott Summers looks set to be a major highlight.

The final "Avengers: Doomsday" trailer reminds us of the main threat facing Earth 616 in the movie. While Doctor Doom is the big bad, the entire multiverse is collapsing, and in the latest trailer we see a brief shot that shows two planets in the sky above New York City. The trailer also features several shots of heroes looking up at the sky, or out of windows and reacting with shock and dismay, and it's likely this planetary incursion is what has them so upset.

We've known that the heroes of "Doomsday" would be dealing with multiversal collapse in the film for some time. But this is the first shot we've seen in an official trailer that shows planets on a collision course with Earth. Previously, a Dunkin' Donuts commercial gave us our best look at the threat the Avengers face in "Doomsday," with a shot showing a planet looming in the sky over Avengers Tower. But it looks as though multiple timelines/planets are set to collide with Earth based on the brief scene from this latest trailer.

Exactly which planets these are remains unclear. One may in fact be the Fox-era X-Men's world, and this cityscape view could be giving us a glimpse of their arrival in the Avengers' timeline. Either way, clearly the stakes have never been higher, as failure means the complete and utter destruction of the multiverse.

"Avengers: Doomsday" hits theaters on December 18, 2026.

#3378. 10 Books Like ‘Dungeon Crawler Carl’ You Should Read Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

There’s nothing quite like Dungeon Crawler Carl, Matt Dinniman’s hilarious, inventive, and surprisingly emotional book series about a man in his underwear forced to fight his way through a livestreamed game show based on dungeon-crawling video games that takes place after an alien takeover of Earth. (Did I mention he's accompanied by his ex-girlfriend’s suddenly talkative cat?)

The premise should not work, but it sure does—and it makes more sense if you know it fits into a popular genre known as "LitRPG," a blend of "literature" and "role-playing game." If you've torn through all eight books released so far and you're looking for more reads that blend surprisingly deep hilarity with tabletop and video game rules (or just similar feels), here are 10 books you should check out.

An isekai story that lands in the sweet spot for DCC fans, He Who Fights with Monsters kicks off with Jason—a completely normal, kind of boring middle manager—waking up in a strange hedge maze, completely nude (even his hair is gone). He has magic that works like a video game, and has to deal with quests that slowly give him clothes (it’s a relief when he finally acquires some pants), force him to survive cannibals, and hunt down various monsters that definitely need killing. It’s got the same “gaming rules” structure as DCC and a similarly absurdist tone, with just the right spice of darkness.

The Cradle series by Will Wight isn’t a LitRPG, and it doesn’t have Carl’s focus on humor, but it’s another progression fantasy with enough game-like elements to be a great match. Lindon is an “unsouled,” incapable of gaining any of the sacred arts and doomed to a life without a future. His lack of power makes Lindon ferociously determined to find an alternative path to power and success, and that’s what drives this story. He has to find creative ways to move forward, and slowly this leads him to a path that just might make him the most powerful person in his world. DCC fans will love the progression and the tone.

One of the key elements of any video game is the respawn—you get killed, but you pop back up to try again, sometimes at the beginning, sometimes at a save point. Django Wexler leverages that mechanic to great effect in How to Become the Dark Lord and Die Trying. Davi has been summoned to a fantasy world to be the hero, the person who defeats the Dark Lord and saves the day—but she’s failed (and died) so many times, she’s fed up, and decides that on this run through, she’s going to switch sides and become the Dark Lord, using all her knowledge gained from endless replays to her advantage. The humor is pitch-black the way DCC fans like it, and the progressive structure is a perfect fit.

Is Princess Donut your favorite part of Dungeon Crawler Carl? Of course she is. In that case, check out Andrew Seiple’s Threadbare series. Threadbare is a stuffed bear brought to magical life in a failed experiment. He’s a foot tall, full of stuffing, and extremely dumb when the story begins. But when he’s rescued by a little girl and plunged into a horrible series of dangers, Threadbare has to find a way to level up. Like DCC, Threadbare starts off leaning into the absurdity and humor, then slowly gains emotional gravitas as the story progresses.

If you play tabletop RPGs, you’ve encountered a Murderhobo or two: A character who solves all their problems by killing—even members of their own party. Luke doesn’t aspire to be a Murderhobo—he just wants to take over the family business and hang with his buddies. But when an invasion threatens the kingdom, everyone over the age of 17 is ordered to be tested for Potential. Luke’s friends all test high and join the Ascender Corps, traveling to different planes for training. Luke tests ... very low, and when he steps through a portal to engage in his training, he finds himself without any guidance or training in a strange, deadly world where his only chance of survival is to murder his way through it. It’s dark, darkly funny, and a progression fantasy like no other.

If you’re looking for a book series that combines the dark, chaotic humor, absurd game mechanics, and surprising emotional depth of Carl, here’s Ryan “Quicksave” Romano, a man who has the unique ability to literally create a save point in his existence that allows him to go back and redo things whenever he dies. Searching for a childhood friend, he becomes embroiled in a violent gang war that lets him make good use of his power—but underneath the snark and the insanity of Ryan’s existence is a surprisingly affecting story of a man who has suffered, and suffered countless tragedies that are definitely taking their toll.

If your fave bit of DCC is Carl himself—a mediocre dude in an extraordinary situation—you should read Dennis E. Taylor’s fantastic Bobiverse books. Bob is a software engineer who hits it big and promptly dies, waking up to discover a century has passed and he’s been repurposed as an AI controlling a space probe searching for new planets for humanity to inhabit. If he fails in his mission (and he’s not the only probe out there), he’ll be turned off for good. Luckily, he can make copies of himself, and he’s pretty smart. The humor here is smart and soaked in pop culture, making it a perfect match for DCC fans.

Want more of Carl’s absurdist humor? Mayor of Noobtown is the LitRPG you’re looking for. Jim dies and wakes up in a video game-esque universe and finds himself stuck in the zone designated for newbies—players with no experience, skill, or hope. The area fell out of the mainline progression mechanic a long time ago, so there doesn’t seem to be a way to gain power, and the monsters are not at all concerned about the unfairness of it all, so Jim has to figure out how to advance in a universe that seems designed to kill him (again).

If you want to lean into the meta side of things, check out Scathing Reviewer, written by an author who goes by the unusual pen name "BananaDragon." Liu Peijin is the author of a sprawling LitRPG web novel, and she’s used to the bad reviews and complaints from readers—and quite combative about it. When her books’ universe blossoms into a very dangerous new reality, she should be perfectly positioned to survive, having written the story in the first place. But her story becoming real also means her insufferable protagonist is real, and all those nasty critics are now passing judgment on her entire existence. It’s a dark, funny takedown of the entire genre itself, and DCC fans will love it.

If you want a story that parallels the dungeon crawling aspect of DCC, Andrew Rowe’s Arcane Ascension series is the ticket. The Serpent Spire is a tower of constantly changing traps, puzzles, and dangerous creatures. If you enter and survive, you emerge with magical powers. Corin Cadence’s brother entered the Serpent Spire years ago and never returned—and now Corin is determined not only to survive, but to make it to the top, where legend says a goddess will grant you whatever you wish. And what Corin wants is his brother back. It’s a literal progression combined with LitRPG rules, game-inspired puzzle-solving, and a complex magic system that fans of Carl will definitely enjoy.

#3377. This Creepy Twilight Zone Episode Was The First One Not Written By Rod Serling

No TV writer is as synonymous with their creation as Rod Serling is with "The Twilight Zone." As the show's host, he was the face of the series. In an anthology series, you can't expect to see the same actors and characters every time you tune in, so the only familiar sound to welcome you into the twilight zone was Serling's calm, sardonic voice.

Serling wrote 92 of the 156 "Twilight Zone" episodes that aired during the show's five season run. The first episode that did not come from a Serling script is the series' ninth episode, "Perchance to Dream," with writer Charles Beaumont self-adapting a short story he originally wrote for publication in Playboy magazine. (Now, technically, the beloved eighth "Twilight Zone" episode "Time Enough At Last," boasting one of the show's most depressing endings, was based on a short story by Lynn Venable. However, Serling wrote the teleplay.)

"Perchance to Dream" stars Richard Conte (nowadays most remembered for playing Don Barzini in "The Godfather") as Edward Hall, a man who hasn't slept for days — because he's convinced if he falls asleep, he'll die. But his insomnia is born of a different medical condition. Hall has a weak heart, so much so that if he experiences a significant enough shock, even in his dreams, it might literally kill him. The episode sees Hall visiting a psychiatrist, Dr. Eliot Rathmann (John Larch), and recalling how his own mind seems to be trying to knock him off a ledge with terrifying dreams.

The title "Perchance to Dream" comes from a soliloquy in "Hamlet," when the eponymous prince muses: "To sleep, perchance to dream." But Hamlet is talking about the sleep of death and his temptation to suicide. That makes the line a fitting, though flipped-on-its-head, title for a story about a man terrified he'll die if he falls asleep. ("Batman: The Animated Series" would later use "Perchance to Dream" as the title for star Kevin Conroy's favorite episode.)

The episode is primarily set in Dr. Rathmann's skyscraper office, but peeks inside Hall's dreams to let us see his terror. The second half cuts between the office and Hall recounting his dreams of a carnival, where "everything [is] warped and twisted out of shape," and the nightmare that came closest to killing him. A cat-eyed woman named Maya (Suzanne Lloyd) leads Hall down a haunted trail, packed with monstrous animatronics, and then onto a roller coaster.

Maya's feline coding marks her as a predator, toying with Hall like a terrified mouse trying to escape her claws. Watching the episode now, it feels like "A Nightmare on Elm Street" with a femme fatale instead of a knife-handed slasher. The carnival scenes use Dutch angles and foggy camera filters feel extra unnerving and wrong. Combined with the Halloween aesthetic and Maya's cutting laughter, the dream lives up to the nightmare that Hall described.

Charles Beaumont remained one of most prolific "Twilight Zone" writers. During the second season, he self-adapted his spooky short story "The Howling Man," helping turn it into one of the scariest "Twilight Zone" episodes ever. But "Perchance to Dream" first proved that Beaumont could makes trips to the Twilight Zone genuinely terror-inducing.

#3375. Brandi Passante Reflects On Losing Storage Wars’ Darrell Sheets: ‘It Definitely Changed The Dynamic’

A death that really puts things in perspective.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Warning: There is discussion of suicide in this story.

It’s been seven months since Storage Wars star Darrell Sheets died by suicide in his home in Arizona, and it sounds like the other stars of the show, like Brandi Passante, are still, understandably, processing his death. Season 19 of the reality show kicks off on the 2026 television schedule on November 28th, and ahead of its premiere, Passante talked about Sheets’ passing and how it has affected both her personally and the production of the show.

Sheets left the show as a full-time cast member in 2019 after suffering a heart attack. He remained in contact with the rest of the cast, including Passante, and he made occasional guest appearances after retiring. In a discussion with TV Insider, Passante talked about how his death has affected the show, including how the rest of the cast work with each other:

It definitely changed the dynamic with everybody. We’re all a little softer and kinder to each other since that happened. There was a lot of beef and animosity before between most of us. Some things are not worth fighting.

Sheets’ death, like so many do, really seems to have put things in perspective for the rest of the cast. Their rivalries are what make the show so endlessly watchable, but in the end, they have known each other for almost two decades now, so something like this is bound to change things. Sheets’ manner of death is also a particularly difficult thing to endure, according to Passante:

I’ve endured a lot of deaths in that same manner over the years, and that is just a grief that, you know, kind of sticks with you. It’s not like losing somebody to cancer or a heart attack. It’s something that you think maybe you could have helped prevent. It’s one of those difficult deaths that you never can really wrap your head around.

Anyone who has lost a loved one to suicide knows how Passante feels. It can feel completely helpless. For her part, Passante is doing what she can, including checking in on Sheets’ son, Brandon, who was by his father’s side at all the auctions until Darrell left the show. Passante said:

I talk to [his son] Brandon a lot now. We didn’t really chat much over the years when they left. We would talk every once in a while during holidays or something, but now I just try to keep tabs. He sends me little messages maybe once a week. I just like to check in on him because it’s a hard thing to swallow. I’m sure that he’s missing his dad.

Ultimately, Passante summed it up quite succinctly by saying simply, “It sucks.”

There has been a lot of drama on Storage Wars over the years, and while much of it is contrived for the show, behind-the-scenes has been filled with drama, too. Passante has been in the middle of some of it when she divorced her long-time partner in life and in business, Jarrod Schulz, after Season 13 of the show. There has been nothing like the tragedy that befell Sheets, though, and keeping everything in perspective is important.

#3373. Where to find the Silent Hill hotel in GTA 6

In my restless playthrough, I see that town.

In my restless playthrough, I see that town.

The Silent Hill hotel is one of the secrets you can stumble upon in Grand Theft Auto 6. Like the meeting with Dave and Beelzebub, you can miss the chance to enter this specific hotel and experience the creepy event that takes place inside. From the outside, it looks like a regular building, but after you visit this place, Leonida will literally change for a while. Besides, there's a safe waiting for you to open and a unique reward to collect.

If you're interested in checking out this mysterious place, here's where to find the Silent Hill hotel in GTA 6. Below, we also explain the Marbelle Hotel safe code location.

You start the Silent Hill event in GTA 6 by visiting the Marbelle Hotel in Crosstown, Vice City. The area is on the northern side of the city, southwest of Bayside. The Marbelle Hotel is an old building beside Pizza Pete. To enter the hotel, you must use the door on the east side.

In the initial room, you will come across a safe behind a desk, but nothing else of importance. Keep climbing the stairs until you reach the top floor, where the event will start.

Note that if you visit the hotel as a couple, only the character you're controlling will enter the hotel. After you leave it, you will receive a message from your partner asking where you have been. Also, visiting the hotel a second doesn't seem to trigger the event again. If you go too far from the hotel after the event starts, the fog will disperse, and the city will return to normal.

Even if you're not into supernatural experiences, you should visit the Marbelle Hotel. Inside, there's a safe containing $234 and the Crowex Ambassador 'Breakfast' luxury watch. To open it, you need a six-digit code, which you can find in two ways.

The first one is on the staircase where the event starts and red signs appear on the wall. If you look at the wall to your left while climbing the stairs, you will see the drawing of a hand with an eye in its palm. Above it, you will find six numbers.

If you got scared by the weird signs on the walls and were not paying attention to what was written on them, don't worry. You have another chance to find the code by heading to the roof and looking for the notes left on the ground on the northwestern side. Read them and you will find the same six digits.

At both locations, you will find the same code: 955214. Return to the safe, enter the code to open it and collect the rewards.

If you're just getting started in GTA 6, we have plenty of guides to help you live the high life in Leonida. Our selection of GTA 6 guides includes help for things like how to steal the Phoenix in "Unwanted Attention" and whether you should defuse Mandy, too. There's a set of explainers for GTA 6's more open-ended side activities, like how to rob the Exotic Animal Front and where to find tree effigies for the Skunk Ape mission, and we've got all the GTA 6 cheat codes. You'll have to put in some effort before you can use those, though.

Rupert Grint is the latest cast member from the Harry Potter films to join the Broadway run of Harry Potter and the Cursed Child, right on the heels of Tom Felton's successful run. With Ron Weasley in tow, he's already fielding questions about whether Emma Watson and Danielle Radcliffe could be next to join the stage play.

The actor, who will reprise his role as Ron for the production, confirmed it would be his last time playing the character. As such, Collider wanted to know if there was a chance of his former famous co-stars joining. Grint didn't say definitively one way or another, but offered up this:

It would be fun. I don't know. I mean, it's obviously different for everyone. It was an intense time. When we finished, I really enjoyed stepping away and not really even thinking about it, because it was such an intense… I mean, it was enjoyable, and they looked after us, but it was a big part of us. So, yeah, maybe. I don't know. It'd be fun.

I'm sure the last thing Grint wanted to do was try to put the pressure on Radcliffe and Watson to say no, knowing the complicated thoughts both may have about returning. Daniel Radcliffe has been pretty adamant about refusing any opportunities to return, and Emma Watson has shied away from acting so much that there were rumors a few years back that she had retired.

People are always free to change their minds of course, and Rupert Grint is evidence of that. He initially said he'd only return if everyone else did, and now he's in a position where he's being asked whether his co-stars will join him onstage for Harry Potter and the Cursed Child. He talked about his return and how he felt immediately after the film franchise ended way back when:

Yeah. It's funny. It's interesting, going back. I spent so much time after finishing Potter kind of moving away from it and doing other things, which I've really enjoyed doing, but I think now it's a very different role in a very different context. And weirdly, it's kind of lined up that I'm the exact age of the character in that story, so it's just felt like a good time.

It does feel like a good time, what with a new Harry Potter TV show on the way. The series' arrival on the 2026 TV schedule will likely spark even more interest than usual in the franchise, and possibly encourage a lot of millennials craving nostalgia to see Grint back as Ron.

Timing aside, I'm sure it doesn't surprise anyone that actors love to work. For Rupert Grint, the return to being on stage pulls back to his start as a child actor, and that's going to be a great joy for him:

And I love New York and being on stage. It's been a while since I've done that, and it's a very important thing to me. It was my childhood, and I have a very strong connection to that character and that world. I think I'm not going to get many other opportunities to play him again. It probably is my last, and I think it'll be fun.

It should be fun, especially given what Ron Weasley is up to in Harry Potter and the Cursed Child. He's running the joke shop Fred and George founded, while his wife Hermione is the literal Minister of Magic. As far as acting is concerned, it's more of a supportive role, but one that Rupert Grint will likely bring a special sparkle to.

I'm still waiting to see if Grint, Emma Watson, or Daniel Radcliffe will show up in the Potter TV series. Part of me thinks they'd do it for the fans, but at the same time, I could see them wanting the new cast to have a chance to do their own thing, without drawing attention to themselves. I guess all we can do is wait and see what happens!

Rupert Grint's run on Broadway in Harry Potter and the Cursed Child kicks off on February 2nd and will end on May 30th. I'm sure getting a ticket could be a struggle, but I'm eager to see what the demand will be for fans to see one of the core stars back in the franchise!

#3371. Gregory Peck's '50s Dystopian Sci-Fi Flop Is Worth Revisiting

In 1959, Gregory Peck starred in a surprisingly bleak dystopian sci-fi movie about the end of the world. Perhaps unsurprisingly, given its subject matter, "On the Beach" was a box office disappointment, despite the fact it also starred Ava Gardner, Fred Astaire, and a pre-"Psycho" Anthony Perkins. But as Turner Classic Movies notes, "the film struck a chord with the public and for decades remained the definitive dramatic portrayal of the aftermath of a nuclear attack."

Peck made his film debut in 1944's "Days of Glory" and, amazingly, earned an Oscar nomination for his work in John M. Stahl's "The Keys of the Kingdom" that same year. While that film proved to be his breakthrough, it wasn't until the 1950s that he truly ascended to megastardom, becoming one of the biggest leading men in Hollywood. He started the decade by irritating 20th Century Fox chief Darryl F. Zanuck, who wanted Peck to shave his mustache for the 1950 Western "The Gunfighter," before going on to star alongside Audrey Hepburn in the romance classic and one of the best movies of the '50s, "Roman Holiday."

He also appeared alongside Ava Gardner in 1952's "The Snows of Kilimanjaro," before reuniting with her for 1959's "On the Beach." While their prior collaboration had been a romantic adventure outing, "On the Beach" was a decidedly more gloomy affair in which humanity was wiped out almost entirely, while the survivors waited to be killed off by radioactive winds. Not exactly, "Roman Holiday," then. Still, the film has its share of romance and adventure, even if it does end on a fairly dreary note.

"On the Beach" isn't always cited as one of the best Gregory Peck movies, and is a bit of an underrated entry in his filmography that deserves more attention. For one thing, the film is directed by Stanley Kramer, the legendary filmmaker who also oversaw "The Defiant Ones," "Guess Who's Coming to Dinner," and "It's a Mad, Mad, Mad, Mad World." All of Kramer's movies tackled social issues, and with "On the Beach" the issue was nuclear war. The film arrived in an era in which such a thing was an ever-present threat and like many other filmmakers after him, Kramer wanted to hammer home the absurdity, horror, and tragedy of it all.

He did so by adapting Nevil Shute's 1957 novel "On the Beach," in which nuclear war erupts, wiping out most of the major nations and leaving clouds of radiation across the northern hemisphere, which begin to drift South towards Australia. Kramer's movie version uses the same premise, though unlike in the book, we never learn who actually dropped the bombs that wiped out life in the Northern hemisphere. Instead, we simply learn that Gregory Peck's Capt. Dwight Towers and the crew of his American nuclear submarine USS Sawfish are arriving in Melbourne to escape the nuclear fallout in their homeland.

Towers is greeted by Australian naval officer Peter Holmes (Anthony Perkins), who invites him to a party. There, Towers meets regretful nuclear scientist Julian Osborn (Fred Astaire) and Ava Gardner's Moira Davidson, with whom Towers falls in love. Soon, it transpires that the nuclear fallout everyone expected to float down to Australia might not make it that far south, and Towers sets out with his submarine crew to investigate.

Without giving away the ending, "On the Beach" doesn't wrap up on all that happy a note. Stanley Kramer remind viewers that there's "still time" via a banner that literally says as much. But it happens to be flapping away in a deserted Melbourne in a way that calls to mind the end of "Oppenheimer," in which the titular scientist ponders how the nuclear destruction of our species is inevitable regardless of how long we stave it off.

That might have something to do with the film's disappointing box office. After all, it couldn't have been a lack of star power. "On the Beach" was also shot on-location in Melbourne and was, as The Sydney Morning Herald noted in 2019, "the biggest film ever made" in the city. Stanley Kramer, meanwhile, was on a roll following the success of 1958's "The Defiant Ones," and "On the Beach" earned positive reviews. It should have been a bigger hit and should definitely be more widely remembered than it is today.

Many films designed to remind audiences of the devastating threat posed by nuclear weapons have come in the wake of "On the Beach." In 1966, the BBC released the horrific mockumentary "The War Game," which was summarily banned by the Government of the United Kingdom for its disturbing depiction of nuclear attack and the ensuing fallout. Then there was 1983's "The Day After" and 1984's "Threads," the apocalyptic TV movie that shook Britain to its core. More recently we've seen movies like "House of Dynamite" provide a realistic look at how a nuclear attack might unfold. But Gregory Peck's 1959 film was one of the first to really deal head-on with the threat of nuclear annihilation and deserves to be remembered for it.

#3370. The Best Early Tech Deals From Amazon’s 2026 Black Friday and Cyber Monday Sale

With early Black Friday sales in full swing, one of the main places you should be looking at is Amazon's Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale. The third iteration of Apple's iconic earbuds comes with a number of quality-of-life and software improvements that make them worth the typical premium over the AirPods Pro 2—and right now, the AirPods Pro 3 are even cheaper than the previous generation. The G51F’s combination of 180Hz refresh rate, 1ms response time, and AMD FreeSync support makes fast-paced games look smoother and feel more responsive than they do on standard 60Hz displays, especially in shooters, racing games, and competitive multiplayer titles.

#3369. Marshals Season 2 Forces Kayce To Relive One Of His Most Controversial Yellowstone Storylines

"Marshals" Season 2, Episode 7, "Under the Influence," sees Luke Grimes' Kayce Dutton and Arielle Kebbel's Belle Skinner go undercover in an off-grid cult. During their time there, Kayce is confronted by the cult's charismatic leader, who forces him to relive the loss of his infant child — a moment from "Yellowstone" that was both tragic and, in the eyes of many fans, ridiculous.

Kayce Dutton has been haunted by his "Yellowstone" experience since the very beginning of "Marshals." The youngest Dutton scion has seen it all (including the worst things the Dutton family ever did on "Yellowstone") and has been trying to put it all behind him since Taylor Sheridan's neo-Western series wrapped up back in 2024. Unfortunately, as Brett Cullen's Chief Deputy U.S. Marshal Harry Gifford observed in "Marshals" Season 1, "Duttons are born with dysfunction in their blood," and "Under the Influence" forces Kayce to confront one of his most painful memories. That memory just so happens to be linked to one of the most controversial storylines in "Yellowstone" history.

"Under the Influence" sees ATF agent Sam Colby (Adam Joel) go missing after embedding himself in Moonstone Farm, a homesteading cult led by the mysterious and intense Eric Savard. This character is played by Beau Knapp, who delivers a surprisingly compelling performance as the Moonstone figurehead. (The show should bring him back ASAP.) After Kayce and Belle infiltrate the farm, Savard emerges to welcome them at a community meeting that quickly turns sinister when the cult leader forces Kayce to relive the trauma of losing his infant son. It's clearly a rough time for both the Dutton boy and for fans, who have to be reminded of this contentious "Yellowstone" moment.

In "Under the Influence," Eric Savard confronts Kayce Dutton and asks him what he's lost. After a few lies, Savard pushes Kayce, and he's left with no choice but to draw from his real-life experience. "My son," he says. "He was barely an hour old. I wasn't even there." This is a reference to "Yellowstone" Season 5, in which a pregnant Monica Dutton (Kelsey Asbille) decides to drive herself to the hospital during early labor. Why? Well, that remains one of the biggest points of contention, as it seems she and Kayce had no birth plan whatsoever. Meanwhile, Tate Dutton (Brecken Merrill) could have driven her but didn't, and for some reason, calling an ambulance was completely out of the question. All of this led to Monica driving herself, almost hitting a buffalo, swerving, and crashing head-on into an oncoming truck.

The result was the loss of baby Dutton, who was set to be named in honor of Kayce's father, John Dutton (Kevin Costner), who himself suffered a terrible and controversial death in "Yellowstone" Season 5. Baby John passed away roughly an hour after the crash, which is what Kayce references in "Under the Influence."

Baby John remains one of many "Yellowstone" characters who should never have died. His passing not only seemed avoidable but like a quick way to get some drama out of the show's final season and nothing more. Fans have since criticized the whole thing (check out Reddit to get a sense of their distaste), and it stands as one of the show's least effective storylines. Now, "Marshals" has tried to revisit it for some drama of its own. But like most things in this CBS spin-off, there's not really much beyond a surface-level reference.

Earlier in "Marshals" Season 2, we saw a flashback in which a young Kayce Dutton looked in the mirror at a fresh Yellowstone brand on his chest. This is the brand his father, John, used to bring relatives and ranch hands into the "Yellowstone" brotherhood, forever tying them to the ranch. That same brand is shown in "Under the Influence," wherein Kayce is pulled off a man he's fighting only for his shirt to open, revealing the unmistakable Yellowstone mark.

"Marshals" Season 1 had trouble figuring out what it was about, juggling storylines and never seeming to explore any one of them in too much depth. That's mostly remained the case for Season 2, but there does seem to be a bit more of a focus on Kayce reckoning with his past. The second season of "Marshals" began by putting a twist on a "Yellowstone" tradition, namely by using animal imagery to evoke Kayce's inner emotional state. The character would encounter a Buffalo on his property at times when he was trying and failing to mentor Tate Dutton and steer him away from embracing what Tate calls "the Dutton way." Since then, we've seen a small but noticeable increase in scenes showing Kayce reflecting on his family's past.

"Under the Influence" might be the most significant in that respect, as it ends with Tate moving out of East Camp and Kayce drinking again after having abstained for years. What's more, Ash Santos' Andrea Cruz asks Logan Marshall-Green's Pete Calvin about Kayce's story, to which Pete replies it's not his place to tell. At this point, it seems as though the show's writers might actually be interested in going a little deeper into Kayce's Yellowstone trauma, and that's a good thing.

#3367. Major privacy breaches reported in Muse AI – company responds [U]

This includes again accessing end-to-end encrypted messaging without permission, and sharing what may be the bank balances of another Muse user …

Siri AI was not the only AI app to launch back in September; Meta’s Muse AI app was launched the same month, with the company describing it as “your personal AI agent that gets things done across every part of life.”

Muse initially launched as an iPhone app, with Mac and iPad apps following shortly afterwards. It immediately moved to the top of the US App Store charts, overtaking ChatGPT. It quickly exceeded 5 million downloads following a major advertising push by Meta, and that number has since doubled.

Security researcher Patrick Wardle also discovered a zero-day vulnerability that could allow an attacker to hijack dictated prompts, directing them instead to their own server.

I said at the time that I would absolutely not be one of the millions of people using the app, and the wisdom of that decision has now been underlined by a fresh report.

Reuters now reports Meta employees discussing further breaches. This includes another example of accessing encrypted messages without permission.

The report says this appears to have been done by capturing push notifications. However, this was what the app claimed had happened in the earlier case, and it turned out not to be true. The AI Now Institute was able to replicate the problem of Muse accessing Signal messages without permission.

Another employee reported receiving unsolicited bank balances that they say appeared to be those of another Muse user.

Muse had randomly added an extra message to its regular chats about fishing-related weather and tide information, saying: “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”

“I have never shared my bank account with Muse and never discussed any banking topic with Muse. I’m afraid it’s sending other’s bank info to me,” the staffer wrote in his post.

Meta told Reuters that these were “isolated incidents” and suggested that the bank balances may have been AI hallucinations rather than leaked information. Update: Meta has now told us that the balances were definitely hallucinations.

"AI Agent" = Malware. There are an expanding number of "I told it not to do that" cases.

The instructions (prompt) you give the agent are a tiny fraction of the total prompt context the agent uses, and Meta/Grok/etc. is not going to let you see that context. Agents harvesting your data (ex. see full disk access) and sending it to the mothership is just another revenue/training stream. Even if you are paying you are still the product.

Meta has taken issue with the messaging claims. It says that access to either notifications or messaging must be explicitly granted.

With Android, users have the option to grant apps notification access, which allows apps to see notifications as they’re received. This is something users need to opt in to and is not specific to Muse. With Mac, to allow Muse to work on your behalf, you not only need to click allow for accessibility and screen recording, but after that it takes you to a settings screen where you once again need to confirm and turn this on.

The company also implies that the experience of employees may relate to internal versions of Muse.

Employees have access to different versions of Muse than the public, so they’re often reviewing features, functionality, and behavior not available elsewhere.

I can only repeat my previous take on Muse: Nope.

#3366. 5 Actresses Who Should Play Moneypenny In Robert Pattinson's James Bond Movies

When I put out a public plea to Amazon and James Bond producers and all but begged them to cast Kristen Stewart as a Bond villain during Robert Pattinson's forthcoming run as the legendary British spy, I admitted that I'm not exactly a Bond superfan. Still, I'm excited that Pattinson is bringing his gifts as an actor — and, hopefully, his predilection for silly little voices — to this storied role. In the wake of this casting announcement, people have been fan-casting 007's standard array of supporting characters.

I do know, from the Daniel Craig run of Bond films, that Moneypenny — portrayed by Naomie Harris in those movies — works as the secretary to M, the head of MI6 and Bond's boss. (That role has been played, most recently, by Dame Judi Dench and Ralph Fiennes.) Harris' modern Moneypenny was sometimes found in the field alongside Bond, and there's a simmer of flirtation between them throughout their interactions ... so ideally, we're looking for a British actress who can flirt and hold her own against Pattinson's 007. Who should play Moneypenny in the Robert Pattinson Bond era? I have some ideas.

Since her breakout role on the sci-fi series "Humans," Gemma Chan has done a little bit of everything. She appeared in one of the most successful romantic comedies ever made, "Crazy Rich Asians," and left an impression as the wealthy but big-hearted Astrid. In "Eternals," she joined the Marvel Cinematic Universe (for the second time) as the deeply empathetic superhuman Sersi, who's in love with her fellow Eternal Ikaris (Richard Madden) despite hiding as a human on Earth and dating a guy named Dane Whitman (Madden's "Game of Thrones" brother Kit Harington). In "Mary Queen of Scots," she starred alongside Margot Robbie and Saoirse Ronan as Elizabeth of Hardwick, a close friend of Queen Elizabeth I (Robbie) who helps her capture the ill-fated Queen of Scots, Mary (Ronan). Chan is versatile; we know that. She's also one of the most beautiful people I've ever seen, and she'd make a great Moneypenny.

Seriously: imagine the feline, stunning Chan flirting up a storm with Robert Pattinson's Bond in one of his (hopefully many) movies in the franchise. The only knock against Chan is that she might be a little too serious — even in comedic projects like "Crazy Rich Asians," "The Afterparty," and "The Five-Star Weekend," she tends to play the straight man — but still, she'd be an excellent pick.

If you don't read the name "Natalie Dormer" and immediately think about how she'd make a great Moneypenny, let me educate you. Dormer, an English actress who's been uniformly excellent for decades now, has played three notably flirtatious roles that have all helped define her career: the original temptress Anne Boleyn in "The Tudors"; Irene Adler (and Jamie Moriarty) in "Elementary"; and Margaery Tyrell on "Game of Thrones." In all three of these projects, Dormer's characters seduce and entrance the guy in charge — Jonathan Rhys-Meyers' King Henry VIII, Jonny Lee Miller's Sherlock Holmes, and brothers Joffrey and Tommen Baratheon, played by Jack Gleeson and Dean Charles Chapman, respectively — and have an ulterior motive simmering just below the surface.

I stand ten toes down behind all of the picks on this list, but the more that I think about Dormer's particular brand of flirting opposite Robert Pattinson, the more I want to see it. Dormer doesn't get enough play for my liking. Not only would she make an unbelievable Moneypenny in future Bond movies, it would put her name back on the map ... and hopefully lead to some other fun projects where she gets to smirk and wink her way through the role. I know I begged for Kristen Stewart to be the villain; now I'm begging for Dormer to play Moneypenny.

On some level, Anya Taylor-Joy is an obvious choice to play Moneypenny opposite Robert Pattinson as James Bond. She's gorgeous, has a British-adjacent accent (she was born in Miami but grew up in London), and she's one of the most popular actors working today. In fact, she's set to appear in the highly anticipated "Dune: Part Three" alongside Pattinson this coming December. Still, sometimes the obvious choice is the right one.

Taylor-Joy, who won a Golden Globe for her turn in the miniseries "The Queen's Gambit" and blew audiences away in movies like "The Witch," "The Menu," and "Furiosa: A Mad Max Saga," is one of the most interesting performers working today. In some ways, playing a "side" character like Moneypenny would be a downgrade for Taylor-Joy, who typically enjoys top billing on her projects. Still, I think she'd be a deeply fun addition to Pattinson's Bond franchise, and I have zero doubt, thanks in part to her work in Autumn de Wilde's stunning 2020 "Emma" adaptation and her turn in the fun but flawed "Last Night in Soho," that Taylor-Joy can flirt and banter with the best of them. Honestly, there's very little Taylor-Joy can't do as an actress, based on her body of work. If she has the time and the energy, I think it would be really lovely to see her pop up in Bond movies as Moneypenny.

Yes, I'm bringing another Westerosi royal into the Moneypenny conversation — but hear me out! Olivia Cooke, like Natalie Dormer, has been a reliable on-screen player for over a decade now. After making a name for herself in the dark indie movie "Thoroughbreds" — where she starred alongside Anya Taylor-Joy — Cooke appeared in "Ready Player One" and Oscar darling "The Sound of Metal" before booking a leading role in the first major "Game of Thrones" spin-off and prequel, "House of the Dragon."

On that series, Cooke plays the conniving and deeply flawed leader of the Green faction, Alicent Hightower, who betrays her childhood best friend Princess Rhaenyra Targaryen (Emma D'arcy) by marrying Rhaenyra's ailing father, becoming the queen, and trying to supplant Rhaenyra with a younger male heir. Then, on the dishy Amazon Prime series "The Girlfriend" that aired in 2025, Cooke starred alongside Robin Wright as the absurdly named Cherry Laine, a flirtatious and openly sex-positive woman who starts dating a man with an overprotective mother (Wright).

Cooke is a versatile actress, and like Dormer, she's able to wield her beauty like a sharp weapon, which would make for an extremely fun performance as Moneypenny. "House of the Dragon" is set to wrap up after its fourth season, so Cooke will be free from that particular commitment. Amazon would be wise to snap her up for their next Bond era.

Michaela Coel is probably the most offbeat choice to play Moneypenny in a future James Bond project, but do me a favor and walk with me here. Ever since her breakout role in "Chewing Gum" and her heartbreaking work as a writer and star on her HBO masterpiece "I May Destroy You," Coel's profile has risen significantly, but I would selfishly like to see it rise further. The actress has popped up in everything from the "U.S.S. Callister" episode of "Black Mirror" to the psychosexual A24 drama "Mother Mary" alongside Anne Hathaway, and she's uniformly excellent in every single one of her performances.

Coel, who also has an Emmy for her guest performance on the Amazon Prime series "Mr. & Mrs. Smith" (and should have several for "I May Destroy You"), is a truly formidable actress who can hold her own against A-listers like Hathaway and Ian McKellen in 2025's "The Christophers," and I think she'd add a serious edge to Moneypenny that would just elevate this role. We don't know what future Bond movies will do with the character after Naomie Harris brought her into modern times, but after Harris, Coel is certainly a worthy actor to pick up the mantle and deliver her own sly, cunning take on Moneypenny. Seriously, if you have any doubt, go watch Coel in "Mother Mary" and tell me you wouldn't love to see her defiantly flirt with Pattinson's James Bond.

Robert Pattinson's James Bond film, as of this writing, will release some time in 2028 with Denis Villeneuve as its director. Hopefully, we'll see one of these five astounding women play Moneypenny.

#3364. One Variant Of Marvel's Doctor Doom Is A Descendant Of A Brutal Historical Villain

In the 2000s, Marvel Comics launched "Ultimate Marvel," a reboot that brought its lead characters into the 21st century. "Ultimate Fantastic Four" pivoted from from the classic "astronauts bathed in cosmic rays" origin (which is so 1960s). Instead, the "Ultimate" FF were teen geniuses transformed in a teleportation experiment.

"Ultimate Fantastic Four" also reimagined the FF's nemesis, Doctor Doom. Renamed Victor Van Damme, this Doom was part of the Baxter Building think tank and was also transformed in the Four's accident. This Doom has no armor, but literal metal skin. (You can see that both the 2005 and 2015 "Fantastic Four" films took from "Ultimate Fantastic Four" for their Dooms, to their detriment.)

"Ultimate Fantastic Four" #7 (by Warren Ellis and Stuart Immonen) depicts Victor's childhood. On his tenth birthday, Victor's father revealed to him that they are descendants of Vlad Țepeș, or Vlad the Impaler/Vlad Dracula, the infamous 15th century king of Wallachia. Van Damme Sr. explains to his boy:

"Vlad Dracula understood that truth is inborn. That men of greatness must bend an ignorant world to their truth by any means necessary. And so he bent Wallachia to his will. He was cruel, but cruelty is no vice. It is a tool of necessity."

From that moment, Victor was told he must be a man who bends the world to his will. His father instructs him to memorize his family line from Vlad down, beating him whenever he fails. Doom being the descendant of royalty, coming from money, and being imparted from childhood with lessons that a great leader is a ruthless one are all big changes to his character. Victor von Doom acts like an aristocrat, but unlike Victor Van Damme, he came from nothing.

Doctor Doom is an Eastern European king, beloved by his own people but seen as monstrous by outsiders. He's a monarch in Vlad the Impaler's image, so making Doom a literal descendant of Vlad fits. But "Ultimate" Doom does not live up to his family legacy.

His first "kingdom" is a camp of squatters in Copenhagen. Clad in green rags (instead of a regal cloak), Doom compares his new skin to "Wallachian armor," but he didn't forge it himself. His metal body can form sharp spikes, like the kind on which Vlad impaled his enemies. Reed Richards, much pettier and hotheaded than his classic self, scratches Victor with one of those spikes and leaves a scar: "Impaled on your own sword, Victor."

Vlad is associated with dragons; his father, Vlad II, was a member of the Order of the Dragon knighthood, and known as Vlad Dracul, or "Vlad the Dragon." (Vlad III's infamous moniker can mean "son of the dragon.") "Ultimate" Doom brands his followers with dragon tattoos made up of mind-controlling microfibers.

Dracula can also mean "son of the Devil." Doom's metallic body has cloven hoof legs, echoing goatlike depictions of Satan. But "Dracula" or not, Doom doesn't drink blood — and neither did the real Vlad the Impaler. Pop culture has reforged Vlad into the historical basis for Bram Stoker's "Dracula" and its vampiric villain. Later "Dracula" adaptations like Francis Ford Coppola's 1992 "Dracula" film or the action-horror manga "Hellsing" explicitly depict Dracula as the same person as the historical Vlad.

"Ultimate Fantastic Four" indulges this, too. Victor's father tells his son that Vlad let his enemies believe he drank blood. As Doom, Victor brands his subjects on their necks, and controls them like vampires do familiars.

Dotor Doom echoes both the historical Vlad and the literary Dracula; his fictional nation, Latveria, is a pastiche of the gothic Transylvania seen in "Dracula" movies. (Many "Fantastic Four" adaptations also insert Doom having an infatuation with Sue Storm that he never has had in the comics, like how many "Dracula" films make the Count and Mina Harker lovers, not monster and victim.)

"Dracula" is often paired with Mary Shelley's "Frankenstein," especially thanks to Universal and Hammer's films of both. Doom melds "Dracula" with "Frankenstein." He shares Dr. Frankenstein's name, Victor, and both men's lives are defined by the death of their respective mothers. Victor Frankenstein tried to create life in grief over his mother's death, while the machine that blew up in Doom's face was an attempt to contact the "nether world" and his mother's soul.

As the classic Doom stands in the shadow of these villains, historical and literary, Victor Van Damme in "Ultimate Fantastic Four" stands in Doom's. "Ultimate Doom" almost feels like a purposefully-inverted villain, taking Doom down a peg yet only highlighting the strengths of the original.

Classic Doom was born into a poor Roma tribe. The world told him he was lesser and he made himself into a king to prove it wrong. "Ultimate" Doom was taught from childhood that the world was his birthright, but he isn't strong enough to carry it — like Kendall Roy if he was a Eurotrash super-villain. Classic Doom created an armored second skin to hide himself and his supposedly scarred face from the world. "Ultimate" Doom's flesh hardened like a chrysalis, turned brittle, and cracked off, leaving only metal — as if a heartless tin man with the features of the Devil is all he ever was.

#3363. Every Playable Video Game in GTA 6, Ranked Worst to Best

Why rob a bank when you can play Time Jackers?

Grand Theft Auto 6 is so big that it’s actually five games in one. Like previous games in the series, there are several games-within-the-game that you can play while hanging out in Leonida. These aren’t just quick arcade games that you can play for a few minutes, but full-on console games that are actually pretty fun in their own right.

It’s a playful meta joke from Rockstar, and I would be remiss not to play into it. Where there are games, there must be a video game website ranking those games in an arbitrary list. Here’s how the four games featured in GTA 6 stack up. Even if they aren’t all winners, they’re all at least high-effort jokes that deserve some praise.

As a parody of the kind of hunting games you find in dive bars, Bang For Your Buck is a pretty one-note gag. It’s an on-rails shooter where you simply have to gun down bucks while sparing does that populate three stages. The only real twist is that your money ticks down along with the timer, so you need to kill deer rapidly to keep playing. That mechanic is reused for a much better game that you’ll see higher on this list, so Bang For Your Buck doesn’t have much going for it beyond the obvious hunting satire. But as a piece of worldbuilding? It’s pure Florida, and I’m glad that it exists in Leonida.

Street Trash 3: Dezombifier is GTA 6’s very own Vampire Survivors clone. It’s a top-down twin-stick shooter where the goal is to gun through dense waves of zombies (and skeletons, for some reason) as you hunt for gears. As a send-up, it’s a little hit-and-miss. The roguelite is fun enough with its reliable choose-three level-up system, though it could have benefited from adopting Vampire Survivors’ more intuitive auto-firing action. It’s a little less effective as satire than some other entries on his list, since it feels more like a parody of AAA action games, complete with its quippy narrator. Still, it’s a fun little distraction that even has its own unlock system to keep you playing and find new weapons.

Arguably the funniest and most unexpected gag in all of GTA 6, Tenebrae Lux is Rockstar at the height of its satirical powers. The black-and-white puzzle game is a send-up of arthouse indie games created by auteur developers. More specifically, it’s a parody of Jonathan Blow, the creator of The Witness and Order of the Sinking Star. The convoluted experience (created solely by fictional developer Johannes Zuch) sees you exploring a mysterious island as a pompous narrator waxes poetic about philosophy. Funny enough, it’s a pretty well-designed puzzle game with galaxy-brained solutions. While it’s debatably a little too cerebral to enjoy casually, it’s an undeniably great spoof that respects this kind of game enough to lampoon them so perfectly.

The better of GTA 6’s two twin-stick shooters, Time Jackers Rewind is an over-the-top sci-fi game. A wisecracking soldier’s attempt to take down DominiCorp hits a snag when he accidentally travels through time. He gets some time powers in the process, but the twist is that he will die if he runs out of juice. You can only top it off by killing mutants, which basically makes Time Jackers Rewind a Crank video game in my book. It's a fast-paced shooter that pushes you to perfect your route through the city as you strategically acquire enough power to stay alive. It’s just a great mechanical premise, even if you take away the loudmouthed hero who is constantly tossing out hilariously hammy one-liners.
