#3361. How To Watch Fjord At Home

Cristian Mungiu's Palme d'Or-winning, Sebastian Stan-starring film "Fjord" will be available to rent on digital platforms beginning November 24, 2026. Given that this is a few days before Thanksgiving, "Fjord" will be the perfect film to watch with the extended family, and won't inspire any kind of snippy, angry political discussions whatsoever.

That, of course, is sarcasm. "Fjord" is, in fact, very, very political. According to /Film's review, "Fjord" is a clumsy, one-sided, and very ideologically weighted drama that is presented as unbiased through its efficient visuals and realistic style, but which is very biased indeed. Even in a room of people who are politically aligned, either to the left or the right, "Fjord" will inspire discussion. Or an argument. Watch it with your politically opposed family members, and let the sparks fly.

"Fjord" tells the story of the Gheorghiu family, which consists of stern Romanian father Mihai (not listed as one of Stan's best roles on /Film's countdown of them) and Norwegian mother Lisbet (Renate Reinsve), along with their two teens, two elementary-school-age kids, and an infant, who move from their long-term Romanian home to the small Norwegian town where Lisbet grew up. The Gheorghius are conservative Christians, which is very different from the local community, mostly made up of non-adherents.

When the Gheorghiu parents are unexpectedly accused of physically abusing their children, Norwegian Child Protective Services immediately takes the kids away (like, in an afternoon), leaving the Gheorghius having to find any kind of legal recourse to get them back. They will eventually have to explain themselves in court. The Gheorghius aren't wholly innocent, confessing to spanking their kids from time to time.

The progressive government of Norway is presented as being full of harridans and busybodies who are hellbent on removing children from their well-meaning parents. "Fjord" presents a political conflict between conservative and liberal ideologies. The Gheorghius attempt to gin up support for their cause by calling in conservative protestors and staging their legal struggle as a bias against Christians. By Romanian social norms, a light spanking is seen as socially appropriate, but the Norwegian government is determined to keep the Gheorghiu kids away from Mihai and Lisbet. The movie sides with the conservative characters, making the entire film feel like light social propaganda.

"Fjord," however, won the Palme d'Or at Cannes, as well as the François Chalais Prize, the FIPRESCI Prize, the Prize of the Ecumenical Jury, and the Prix de la Citoyenneté. It is also beloved by most critics, racking up a 91% approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes, based on 165 reviews. Justin Chang's review in The New Yorker noted that some of the villains in "Fjord" are unrealistically larger-than-life, but that it was ultimately subtle. He wrote:

"Is 'Fjord' guilty, as some have charged, of stacking the moral decks in the Gheorghius' favor? We are presented with a few potentially hissable villains ... Yet Mungiu has an uncommon ability to temper bluntness with nuance."

As soon as it's easily available to rent online, one can watch "Fjord" for themselves and see if it's politically charged, naturally neutral, or morally complex. Cristian Mungiu tends to handle politically difficult issues with frankness and directness; he reminded us of the necessity of abortion with his 2007 drama "4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days." You, however, are the one can must decide if "Fjord" is as powerful.

#3360. Canva introduces new controls to hide generative AI features

In light of growing pushback from users who want more control over how AI is integrated into their apps (if at all), Canva is introducing new settings that let them hide generative AI features and see less AI-generated content. Here are the details.

Canva today announced new controls that will let Free and Pro users choose whether to see generative AI features across the app, as well as how much AI-generated content appears in search results and in recommendations for templates and design elements.

The company notes that both controls are available at no additional cost and can be turned on or off at any time.

According to Canva, “the future of creativity isn’t a choice between AI and no AI.” For this reason, it is introducing the following controls:

The company says that, while it knows that there is an ongoing debate between users with opposing views on whether AI has a place in creative work, it thinks “both views are valid”:

“It’s not our place to tell anyone how to create, so today we’re launching two new controls that put that decision firmly with our community […].”

Importantly, the company noted that select features that use AI without generating new content will remain available even when generative AI features are turned off:

“Some of Canva’s everyday editing tools use AI to make simple tasks faster, without generating anything new. Background Remover, one of Canva’s most popular tools, lifts a subject cleanly out of a photo in a single click, and Magic Grab lets creators select an object in an image and move it somewhere else in the design. Both remain available when the generative AI switch is off, because they work only with what’s already in a design.”

Canva added that these tools also won’t add an AI label to a design’s metadata, since that label is reserved for AI-generated content.

As for the company’s design content library, Canva said that while “a small portion of the library is AI-generated content made by Canva, including some abstract backgrounds and illustrated graphics,” its community has told it “they want an easier way to find design assets made by real people, so the content control reduces the number of AI-generated templates and elements that appear in search results and recommendations.”

With today’s announcement, Canva is essentially expanding on the AI permissions already available to administrators of Business, Enterprise, Teams, and Education accounts, which let organizations control how their teams use AI.

#3358. 10 Shows Like 'MobLand' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Crime dramas often attract big stars, and MobLand is no exception. The Paramount+ series stars Tom Hardy as mob fixer Harry Da Souza, with Pierce Brosnan and Paddy Considine in supporting roles and Helen Mirren having a ball as the thoroughly evil matriarch of the Harrigan crime family.

While families are complicated in even the best of circumstances, that's especially true of the Family. After you've watched the recently released second season of MobLand, try one of these other shows mixing crime and family (or Family) drama.

Theo James plays army officer Eddie Horniman (a name mentioned as often as possible), heir to the Horniman estate (there it is again) who, upon the death of his father, is named the Duke of Halstead. He learns that his dad was tied to various criminal enterprises, and that his scouse brother is millions of pounds in debt to a drug dealer. What else is the dapper, military-trained Duke to do but learn to navigate the violent underworld while looking cool? You won't be surprised to learn that this British crime drama comes from creator/writer/producer Guy Ritchie, who also has a hand in MobLand. Stream The Gentlemen on Netflix.

Another series from Taylor Sheridan (the Yellowstone guy), this pandemic-era hit stars Jeremy Renner as Mike McLusky, head of a family that’s been keeping the peace, through means fair and foul, in the title's company town for decades. The "business" of the corrupt burg happens to be incarceration, and the McLuskys thrive when business is up, even if Mike has slightly different ideas about how to run things. The show deals broadly with systemic racism and inequality in the prison system, but mostly it's a modern-day western about bringing justice to a corrupt town. It will conclude with a fifth season, streaming in 2027. Stream Mayor of Kingstown on Paramount+.

A consistently compelling combination of smart plotting and lurid sex and violence, Banshee stars Antony Starr as Sheriff Lucas Hood...kinda: He's actually a man recently released from prison who takes over that identity when the new sheriff in the small town of Banshee is killed before anyone really has a chance to get to know him. It's all part of a complicated plan to reunite with his lover Ana (Ivana Miličević), and to get back the $15 million in diamonds he lost when he went to jail—but the town is ruled over by various criminal factions, and being sheriff doesn't guarantee any kind of safety; rather, the opposite. Stream Banshee on HBO Max.

MobLand creator Ronan Bennett previously made this acclaimed series that succeeds by maintaining a narrow scope—in this case, a single London council estate. Dushane (Ashley Walters) and Sully (Kane Robinson) are residents and drug dealers at Summerhouse, maintaining an increasingly precarious grip on the criminal element in the community. Most compellingly, the series maintains an extensive supporting cast of locals both in the drug trade and impacted by it, building a disturbingly compelling world. A little confusingly, the first couple of seasons were renamed Top Boy: Summerhouse when the show moved to Netflix, so you'll want to start there before moving on to plain ol' Top Boy. Stream Top Boy: Summerhouse on Netflix.

Based loosely on a nonfiction work investigating the Mafia-like Camorra in Campania, this show focuses on the head of the Savastano clan, Pietro Savastano (Fortunato Cerlino), and his ambitious lieutenant Ciro Di Marzio (Marco D'Amore). When Pietro is arrested at the series' outset, a civil war erupts between family members and among the factions vying for control. Gone are the suits and poker games of many a mob drama—this is a brutal, street-level take on organized crime that forsakes the typical trappings of the genre. Stream Gomorrah on HBO Max.

I'm here for the Pierce Brosnan of it all, but there's also a very strong vibe match in this series that casts the one-time James Bond actor as the head of a literal crime family, even if this one's set in the American West. Adapting Philipp Meyer's 2013 Pulitzer Prize-nominated novel of the same name, the series follows Eli McCullough, a ruthless cattle baron making moves to get in on the burgeoning oil industry in the Rio Grande Valley of 1915. A parallel narrative sees Eli as a young man, kidnapped and raised among a Nʉmʉnʉʉ family. While his backstory lends the character welcome complexity, in the present, he's as determined to build his empire as he is to prepare his son and grandson to take over when he's gone. Stream The Son on Prime Video.

Tom Hardy playing a tough guy isn't terribly unexpected, but here the setting is London, just after the end of the War of 1812. Hardy plays James Delaney, who returns from Africa after ten years away (he says he'd been taken prisoner, but his story doesn't entirely add up) for the funeral of his father. Dad left nothing but a little hunk of land off of Vancouver, not worth much until the war's conclusion creates new maritime trade opportunities. Suddenly, the United States, Great Britain, and the East India Company all have eyes on the real estate, and all are willing to do whatever it takes to acquire it—and the stakes become clear once James realizes that his father's cause of death wasn't natural. Stream Taboo on Peacock and Tubi.

Best not ponder too much on the fact that this one's based on a video game, as its pedigree is only hinted at via the levels of action and violence (certainly compared to some of the other shows on this list). Colm Meaney plays Finn Wallace, the absolutely indispensable leader of London's criminal underworld, a man who's been holding everything together for decades, until his shocking murder at the outset of the series (that's not a spoiler, and we spend more time with him via flashbacks). The completely random killing by someone who had no idea what he was doing begets chaos and open violence. Finn's son Sean (Joe Cole) has been raised to take his father's place, but local, Pakistani, and Albanian gangs all move in to take control from the Finn family in the power vacuum. Stream Gangs of London on AMC+.

The great Forest Whitaker stars as the real-life Bumpy Johnson, who returned from a prison sentence to find his neighborhood falling apart and in the grip of Italian mobsters. A more than capable crime boss in his own right, Johnson resolves to take on the Genovese crime family, eventually forming a tentative alliance with Malcolm X (Nigél Thatch and, later, Jason Alan Carvell). Johnson is the lesser evil as far as Malcolm and others are concerned, and a complicated figure as both crime lord and family man with aspirations of saving his neighborhood. The show will conclude with a two-hour finale, likely airing in 2027. Stream Godfather of Harlem on Hulu.

Adopted into an Italian organized crime family as a baby, Park Joo-hyung took on the name Vincenzo Cassano, eventually becoming a mafia consigliere. After his adoptive father Don Fabio dies, Fabio’s biological son comes gunning for his brother, whom he now sees as competition. Cassano flees to Seoul, on the hunt for a secret stash of money, and in the process discovers a love interest and a new adversary in a giant business conglomerate that definitely deserves to be taken down. An incredibly popular K-drama, this one definitely puts a unique spin on the tropes of the mob genre. Stream Vincenzo on Netflix.

#3357. Jane Fonda on Documentary ‘Gaslit,’ Trump, and What the Democrats’ Midterm Victory Means for Climate Change

In “Gaslit,” a new documentary about climate change activists, Jane Fonda stands outside one of Formosa Petrochemical’s Texas facilities and looks through a thermal camera. The Oscar-winning actress is brought to tears by what she sees: a tremendous expulsion of methane gas into the air.

“Methane is 80 percent more destructive to the climate, in terms of global warming, than carbon dioxide,” Fonda explained during a recent Zoom interview. “It’s the most destructive chemical that we’re using, and it’s extremely dangerous for people. And yet here it is billowing into the air, and nobody even knows it.”

For years, Fonda has been sounding the alarm about the looming environmental catastrophe that will take place if the world doesn’t wean itself off fossil fuels. She launched a series of climate change protests dubbed “Fire Drill Fridays” in 2019 — a reference to activist Greta Thunberg’s charge that people should “act as if your house is on fire” — and has been arrested multiple times for civil disobedience. Fonda is embracing the cause with the same passion that has led her to speak out on everything from the Vietnam War to feminism to LGBTQ+ rights. But she worries her efforts may not be enough. Related Stories Paul Thomas Anderson’s ‘Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall’ Getting Nationwide Release in January Rian Johnson Leaves the Door Open to Star Wars Return: ‘It’s a World I Deeply Love’

“Our emission of global warming chemicals has gone way up since Donald Trump has become president,” Fonda said. “And of course the concern is always: Have we passed too many tipping points or a tipping point? Many climate scientists say if we act fast now, it won’t be too late. But it’s very hard to act fast when Trump is president.”

The political winds are changing. The midterms were a blue wave election that saw Democrats take back the House and the Senate in commanding fashion. They not only performed well in liberal bastions, but also captured the governor’s mansion in Texas and elected James Talarico to a U.S. Senate seat that has been in Republican hands for decades. Much of “Gaslit” focuses on the environmental damage wrought by the oil fields in West Texas’ Permian Basin. Will the change in leadership make a difference?

“It won’t hurt,” Fonda said. “I don’t know how strong Talarico is on these issues. We can’t do too much until our members are seated, and we actually have the majority in the House in January.”

“Renewables are ready,” she added. “They’re cheap. They’re safe. They’re job-intensive. It’s the perfect solution. It’s right there. It makes all the sense in the world. The only thing we lack is political will, and hopefully, with this swath of new people that have been elected to the House and the Senate, we will have the political will when we take power to turn this around.”

Fonda believes average citizens concerned about climate change can’t afford to be passive.

“One of the most important things that people can do is to demand that their elected officials pass legislation that makes these polluters pay for what they’re doing,” Fonda said. “Right now, it’s consumers, it’s us taxpayers that have to pay for the damage. They should pay, and we have to stop the $21 billion annual subsidies that we pay them. They make trillions of dollars of profit. If we cancel those subsidies, it would spell the beginning of the end for fossil fuels.”

Fonda is blunt in her warnings that the chaos and damage that global warming has caused will only accelerate unless the world switches to renewable sources of energy. Her assessment is sober, even terrifying, but one thing that gives her hope is the work that the activists highlighted in “Gaslit” are doing. “Gaslit” was financed and produced by the environmental group Greenpeace USA, and it focuses on people in the Gulf Coast and Texas who are trying to change things across the political spectrum. They range from a Republican cattle rancher, who has seen what the oil and gas business has done to his family’s land, to cancer survivors and community organizers who are hoping to change hearts and minds about fossil fuels.

“What is so moving to me about the film is we’re showing these people who do not give up; they will not,” Fonda said. “All of these activists are so brave and so incredible. They inspire me.”

“Gaslit” was directed by Katie Camosy. It is now available to rent or buy on Amazon Prime and Documentary+. As of November 19, the film can be streamed on the Greenpeace USA YouTube channel, with additional platforms rolling out.

#3356. Forget Yellowstone, Taylor Sheridan's New Show Is Officially Less Than A Month Away

Faith Roswell is a Senior Writer on Screen Rant's Classic TV team. Since earning her degree in Creative Writing over a decade ago, Faith has written articles on film and TV from a variety of different angles. Faith now combines her knowledge of psychology with her love of monster movies to give more insight into what makes the best ones.  You may have read her Screen Rant lists and features covering horror, sci-fi, and fantasy, or read her Amazon Top 10 book, "Movie Monsters of the Deep." Faith has had an extensive career as a writer, appearing on BBC live radio, researching true crime for Rotten Mango podcast, and writing for publications including Mental Floss, Atlas Obscura, and The Daily Jaws before beginning here at Screen Rant.

Taylor Sheridan's directorial debut instantly made him a force of nature in one main genre, with the Yellowstone franchise widely credited with reviving the Western genre for a modern audience. Since then, Taylor Sheridan's TV shows have gone from strength to strength, with the Yellowstone TV shows reaching into the past through prequels, and with spinoffs like Dutton Ranch being hits with both critics and audiences. However, while Sheridan's Westerns might have made his career, he has been slowly expanding into another genre, with his biggest leap coming next month.

Mayor of Kingstown had elements of a great neo-Western TV show, but it marked Sheridan's departure into the crime thriller genre. Then, after a return to Yellowstone's world with its prequel,1883, Tulsa King then continued his crime thriller run but brought comedy into the mix, with Sylvester Stallone's performance as the relocated mafia capo Dwight Manfredi bringing new viewers to Sheridan's TV shows. Now, the director is building on this success with Frisco King, which arrives on Paramount+ on December 18. This continues an extraordinary career streak, as Sheridan has several upcoming TV shows in the pipeline.

The only Taylor Sheridan TV show to receive negative Rotten Tomatoes ratings from critics and audiences is Marshals. Considering the fact that the director has been central to making 14 TV shows in the past eight years, this is a remarkable achievement. 1923 and Landman polarized Rotten Tomatoes critics and audiences, with critics awarding both shows 94% and 80% ratings respectively, and audiences being considerably less impressed. That said, even this indicates that these shows are fuel for discussion and debate, rather than being forgettable, and both 1923 and Landman still won Satellite Awards.

Sheridan's prestige TV shows follow a formula that allows for creativity without forcing any to feel same-y. His characters tend to be morally ambiguous but deeply connected to their setting, allowing for extensive worldbuilding and requiring nuanced performances from the cast. The acting in Taylor Sheridan's TV shows is consistently excellent, as his shows have attracted some of the most accomplished actors working today, from Helen Mirren to Zoe Saldaña. Now Frisco King is being headed by another megastar, with Samuel L. Jackson in the main role as a gangster who relocates to the suburb of Frisco, Texas.

Frisco King is a sequel to Tulsa King, which is a fish-out-of-water crime comedy centering on Dwight "The General" Manfredi, who is released after a 25-year prison sentence and sent to Tulsa, Oklahoma to set up a new life away from his mafia contacts. However, old habits die hard and before long, Manfredi is setting up his own criminal enterprise. Tulsa King's third season introduced Russell Lee Washington Jr (played by Jackson,) as an old friend and prison mate of Manfredi, now working as a New York hitman. After refusing the order to kill Manfredi, he also decides to relocate.

Samuel L. Jackson's best movies and TV shows have been crime staples, and his performance was one of Tulsa King's standouts. This makes Frisco King feel like a logical next step for the story and characters, and Stallone is reprising his role as Manfredi for a few episodes, acting as a familiar face to help introduce the new series and its tone, which will be different from Tulsa King. Rather than repeat the original show's story with a different character, the sequel is set to move further toward comedy, marking an even more drastic genre change from Sheridan's neo-Western beginnings.

Tulsa King's Dwight Manfredi is Sylvester Stallone's first role in a scripted TV series.

While Frisco King does not directly connect to any more of Taylor Sheridan's TV shows other than Tulsa King, it shares directors Christina Alexandra Voros and Michael Friedman with Yellowstone, as Sheridan has split directing duties across the show's eight episodes, while writing each of the episodes himself. With this new show on the horizon, Sheridan's Tulsa King franchise is finally taking shape, and Frisco King marks another major change for the director, establishing him as a multi-genre powerhouse with another potential hit franchise on his hands. ​​​​​

#3355. Nintendo's Black Friday Deals Are Actually Pretty Good

Black Friday is nearly upon us. From now through Cyber Monday, retailers and companies alike are offering deals and discounts on their wares. While I always keep an eye out for Nintendo deals offered by stores like Amazon, Best Buy, and Walmart, it seems the company is offering its own discounts this year—and, surprisingly, they're actually pretty solid.

Last Thursday, Nintendo announced its Black Friday discounts. We've already seen Switch 2 sales ahead of the Black Friday season, but now, Nintendo has confirmed an official discount for the console.

Starting Nov. 22 through Dec. 5, you can pick up Nintendo's Switch 2 Mario Kart bundle for $499.99, down $50 from $549.99. That includes the console, a download of Mario Kart World, and a 90-day Nintendo Switch Online Individual Membership.

If you already have a Switch 2 console and/or Mario Kart World, you're not left out of the Black Friday deals here. From Nov. 22 through Nov. 29, Nintendo is also running discounts on several high-profile Switch and Switch 2 games:

Donkey Kong Bananza was one of Nintendo's launch titles for the Switch 2. And while it's been out for over a year, Donkey Kong's first 3D game is still among the best-reviewed titles on the console. Nintendo is taking $30 off the game's MSRP for this promotion.

Kirby Air Riders on Switch 2 is only the second installment in the series. The original launched all the way back on the GameCube, and while the title typically runs for $69.99, Nintendo is letting it go for $39.99.

Metroid Prime 4 arrived last year after an 18-year wait from Metroid Prime 3: Corruption. The game typically retails between $59.99 and $69.99 for a physical copy, but Nintendo is selling it for $39.99 during its early Black Friday promotion.

Super Mario Galaxy (both the original and the sequel) are beloved by fans. These titles originally launched on the Wii, and Nintendo rereleased both for the Switch. (The company offers a free upgrade to the Switch 2 edition.) Nintendo asks $69.99 for this combo, and while you can find it for under $60, you'll officially be able to pick it up for $39.99 before Black Friday.

Nintendo's latest Mario Party, Jamboree, has a Switch 2 edition with a rather staggering MSRP of $79.99. While it's the version of the game with the most features, it's also the most expensive. You'll be able to buy it for $39.99 for Black Friday, saving up to $40.

Nintendo rarely offers official discounts on some of its biggest titles, especially in this current era. In addition, Nintendo announced a sale on its digital store that runs from Nov. 19 through Dec. 2, though it didn't say which titles would be on sale. Just keep an eye on all these dates: The Switch 2 console promotion runs longer than the physical and digital games discounts, while the digital sale runs longer than the physical sale. Nintendo says that these discounts will be available "at select retailers," as well as its brick-and-mortar locations in New York and San Francisco. You can also buy the Switch 2 bundle through Nintendo's website.

It depends! Its Nintendo Switch 2 bundle deal runs from Nov. 22 through Dec. 5; the select games listed above will be on sale from Nov. 22 through Nov. 29; and digital titles will have discounts from Nov. 19 through Dec. 2.

While we don't know which digital titles will be discounted yet, we do know that physical copies of Donkey Kong Bananza, Kirby Air Riders, Metroid Prime 4: Beyond, Super Mario Galaxy + Super Mario Galaxy 2, and Super Mario Party: Jamboree will be on sale for $39.99 each.

Yes! The Switch 2 alone costs $499.99, so you essentially get the game for free. Mario Kart World is also one of the console's best multiplayer titles right now, so it makes sense to pick it up in this bundle.

#3354. Steam Officially Launches Its 2026 Game of the Year Awards Voting

The Golden Joysticks has already weighed in on 2026's Game of the Year and The Game Awards has revealed its nominees for this year's best of the best. But one awards ceremony stands apart from the typical Game of the Year awards contest: the Steam Awards.

On Monday, Valve opened up nominations for its fan-voted awards, which include Game of the Year and what promises to be a highly contested category: the Hall of Fame Award. That brand-new category will pit a list of winners of the Steam Awards’ Game of the Year category from the past 10 years against each other to celebrate a decade of Valve's awards.

From now until Monday, Nov. 30 at 10 a.m. PST, Steam users can vote on the following categories, in addition to the Hall of Fame Award.

The final nominees will be revealed, and voting for the 2026 Steam Awards will begin, on Thursday, Dec. 17. That same day, the Steam Winter Sale kicks off. That's one week to the day after The Game Awards 2026, meaning that if any PC game was slighted by that awards ceremony, Steam users will have a chance to rebuke the TGAs voting body. (One thing that Steam Awards voters won't get to weigh in on is this year's GOTY frontrunner, Grand Theft Auto 6. Rockstar Games hasn't announced a PC version of the game yet.)

Last year's Steam Awards Game of the Year was Hollow Knight: Silksong. Other big winners from last year's Steam Awards include Baldur’s Gate 3, Hades 2, Peak, Silent Hill f, Arc Raiders, and Clair Obscur: Expedition 33.

#3353. OLED iMac plans may be cancelled by Apple for two reasons

Apple is considering abandoning plans to launch an OLED iMac, according to a new supply chain report. The news comes just weeks after the first OLED Mac was launched in the form of the new touchscreen MacBook Pro.

The company is said to be holding discussions with display partner Samsung about either delaying the planned launch or abandoning it altogether, with two reasons cited …

Bring back a pro level iMac. The 27” 5k display was a very good size, make it a more accurate OLED display combined with the latest Apple Silicon, so former iMac owners have a choice where there is none now.

The all In one form factor remains convenient for labs, classrooms, creative departments, audio studios (home & pro), etc.

Keep the non OLED 24” display format positioned as a consumer model, plus lower its cost and you will see a sales uptick.

Apple’s journey into OLED screens began with the Apple Watch while other products were still using IPS LCD. The company subsequently switched to OLED for some iPhones and iPads before a long-awaited launch of the first OLED MacBook Pro back in October.

It was expected that the company would gradually transition to OLED across the full range of Macs over time. However, this process was expected to take a number of years, with the iMac not likely to join the party until 2029 or 2030.

The Elec today reports that the move may be delayed even further or even abandoned altogether, for two reasons: cost and demand.

The company is said to be discussing a potential delay or cancellation of the project with Samsung Display. High OLED panel costs and weak sales of existing OLED-equipped products are believed to be factors behind the reconsideration […]

The biggest factor behind the review is cost. The iMac sells in smaller volumes than smartphones or laptops, making it difficult to maintain competitive pricing if expensive OLED panels are adopted. Weak sales of the OLED iPad Pro are also believed to have influenced the decision.

The report suggests that incoming CEO John Ternus has been reviewing the commercial viability of upgrading more products to OLED. As further evidence, the report says Apple has sent quotation requests to LCD suppliers for an iMac screen to be launched in around 2029.

#3352. ‘Focker In-Law’ Review: An Eager Ariana Grande Isn’t Enough to Save a Comedy Sequel That Can’t Remember What People Liked About This Franchise

The world may not have been champing at the bit for another “Meet the Parents” sequel with quite the same enthusiasm that defined the hype for “GTA VI” (pretty close, tho!), but anyone who’s been itching for another crazaaaazy weekend between neurotic nurse Gaylord “Greg” Focker and his imperious ex-CIA father-in-law Jack Byrnes has had to wait even longer for their prayers to be answered. Was it worth it?

Well, let’s do a quick comparison between two cultural phenomenons that I’m definitely not just lumping together in a desperate — some might say “heroic” — attempt to write an involving review lede for a movie that never makes even the slightest effort to earn your attention. Related Stories Jane Fonda on Documentary ‘Gaslit,’ Trump, and What the Democrats’ Midterm Victory Means for Climate Change Paul Thomas Anderson’s ‘Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall’ Getting Nationwide Release in January

Ahem: On the one hand, it took 13 years for Rockstar Games to produce another numbered installment of their marquee franchise, during which time they leveraged cutting-edge technology and unprecedented financial resources in order to radically iterate upon a proven formula so that the company’s Baudrillardian allegory of American pathos would map onto an era that has become too shattered for more coherent sense-making. On the other hand, it took 16 years for the combined power of Universal and Paramount (a Skydance Company) to will another “Focker” movie into existence, during which time someone realized that it might be kinda funny if Robert De Niro said the words “Jamba Juice.”

And in fairness, they weren’t wrong. A Robert De Niro character shouldn’t know what Jamba Juice is, let alone want to drink there! Not only that, but he correctly emphasizes the “JAM” of it all, the formal precision of which suggests that Jack — a red-blooded Boomer who’s recently become an exercise-obsessed vegan health nut — has developed a sincere degree of respect for the smoothie chain and its various blended offerings, even if it’s taken him 16 years to do so.

Given that John Hamburg’s “Focker In-Law” brings back so much of the franchise’s original cast almost three decades since they first played these roles, the film benefits from a Linklater-esque sense of temporal continuity that invites us to imagine the time between movies as a living space. Don’t be fooled by the gruel-thin story, the parade of self-amused callbacks, or the painfully contrived jokes that substitute for real emotion, this isn’t an opportunistic cash-grab meant to capitalize on our collective appetite for big screen comedies — it’s a family reunion.

the expectations for a legacy sequel are much lower than they might be for the most expensive video game in history, especially in the context of a franchise that’s sustained by the idea that the surname “Focker” sounds almost indistinguishable from the word “fucker.” (Don’t be embarrassed if you hadn’t put that together before — it’s subtle, and film critics are professionally trained to identify such things). “GTA VI” had to revolutionize interactive entertainment in order to be considered a success. “Focker In-Law” just has to deliver more of the same. It does that over and over and over again; I don’t know about Jack’s nipples, but Greg (Ben Stiller) can certainly milk an old joke until it turns to dust in his hand.

The cinematic equivalent of half-rotten Thanksgiving leftovers that you’d only eat in lieu of having any other food in the house, “Focker In-Law” might be an increasingly rare big-screen comedy, but it’s endowed with the “whatever”-level apathy of the worst straight-to-streaming junk. Depressingly, that feels like a systemic failure more than a creative one, as Hamburg is a very funny guy who directed several of the better comedies of this century’s pre-Netflix era (e.g. “Along Came Polly”), and he’s far from the only proven talent who gets wasted here.

The basic story — for which Hamburg shares credit with Austen Earl and, curiously, Ilana Glazer — offers a natural riff on the franchise’s initial premise: Greg might wear Radiohead t-shirts and sport facial skin tighter than any scene in the movie around him, but he’s now older than Jack was during the first movie, which means he and his wife Pam (Teri Polo, making the easiest money of her life) have aged into the “Parents” who are due to be “Meet”-ed when their son Henry (an overqualified Skyler Gisondo) brings his big-eyed new girlfriend Olivia (Ariana Grande) to Jack’s 80th birthday celebration.

The joke, and it’s not a bad one, is that Greg — a beta male bozo who’s desperate to make his children and their partners feel welcome — immediately bumps against his probable daughter-in-law, while Jack — a dominant and unyielding patriarch whose “Circle of Trust” is harder to crack than a captured enemy spy — cottons to her from the moment she gets to his house. It helps, of course, that Olivia is an ultra-rigid life coach and former hostage negotiator who shares Jack’s taste for military discipline, as well as his knowledge of different polygraph technologies. Why she’s drawn to a softboi like Greg’s son remains unclear, but the “Wicked”-like theatricality of Grande’s performance is farcical enough for such open questions to be their own reward (it makes sense that her character would be so emotive and intentional), and at the end of the day what matters is just that Greg has a reason to feel rejected all over again.

He doesn’t take it well! In fact, he acts like a massive asshole about it to a degree that steers the movie away from cringe comedy comfort food and closer towards a character study about a malignant narcissist instead. Stiller is a maestro of self-involved unpleasantness (his work in “Greenberg” and “The Meyerowitz Stories” has never gotten the recognition it deserves), but that kind of toxicity is far more unpleasant in the context of a film that thinks it’s cute and/or easily redeemable.

In “Meet the Parents,” Greg got into all sorts of wacky trouble because he meant well and cared so much about seeming worthy of Jack’s daughter. In “Focker In-Law,” the hijinks stem from the fact that he’s a scheming monster who’s trying to sabotage his son’s relationship so that Henry might stay closer to home. The clean and simple fun of watching good intentions curdle into misunderstood chaos has been replaced by the dull ache of watching someone try to pass off diagnosable psychosis as the stuff of routine parental anxiety.

Alarm bells start ringing from the very first comic setpiece, in which a classic setup — Greg tries to cut the airplane bathroom line by sneaking from coach into first class — is almost completely undone by the logic gaps that have come to define the character. Why does he impulsively steal Olivia’s birth control out of her bag before he even knows who she is, and how is it possible that such an overbearing dad hasn’t even seen a picture of his son’s very serious new girlfriend? Such questions aren’t really worth answering, and Hamburg at least has the courtesy to distract us from them with a fly-by cameo by Cole Escola, but the vibe is all the way off by the time we even touch down in New Jersey for the main event, and nothing that happens there is remotely inspired enough to redeem the pervasive sense that no one can remember why “Meet the Parents” became a franchise in the first place.

Was it Owen Wilson’s amusingly oblivious performance as Pam’s charmed ex-fiancé, Kevin? There’s only one way to find out! Was it Jack’s penchant for lie-detector tests or his affinity for unlovable pets? Let’s give them both a shot and see what sticks. (I was amused by the German shepherd he trains in this film, who sets up a very good joke accusation that I don’t want to spoil here). Maybe it became a phenomenon because people crave manic setpieces that end in a plume of human ashes — we should run that back just in case. Anything to avoid the obvious and enduring coziness of a “home for the holidays” movie, which “Focker In-Law” inexplicably forfeits by setting its story at the height of summer.

The ballad of Gaylord Focker certainly didn’t become a thing because of Greg’s daughter and her long-term boyfriend, whose presence this movie struggles to accommodate despite the fact that Beanie Feldstein and Eduardo Franco are both eager to help liven things up. In fairness, why open the floor to potentially amusing new characters when you can spend half the film’s runtime agonizing over Greg’s uncomfortably demented attempts to steal the engagement ring that Henry wants to give to Olivia? Some opportunities are just too good to pass up, I suppose.

That “Focker In-Law” maintains any of its series’ long-faded charm can be attributed to De Niro, who sleepwalked through the previous two sequels but feels revived by Jack’s newfound looseness in this one. The actor delights in playing off Grande’s type-A eagerness, just as his character takes a muted pleasure in how much Olivia causes Greg to crash out. In a comedy as flat, stilted, and generic as this one, De Niro’s still-inimitable star power is almost enough to save the movie from its own reheated cynicism. “JAM-ba Juice.” They actually just go by “Jamba” now. The franchise’s juice is long, long gone.

Universal Pictures will release “Focker In-Law” in theaters on Wednesday, November 25.

#3351. Now These Apple Services Are Down

If you're having trouble accessing certain Apple products and services today, you are not alone. As of early Tuesday afternoon, Downdetector shows user reports of issues across multiple Apple services. While Apple's System Status page initially showed far fewer issues than Downdetector users reported, the site has since updated to reflect general outages.

According to users on Downdetector, there are currently outages or interruptions to the following Apple services, in order of most to least reported: Apple Support, Apple Pay, iCloud, App Store, Apple Business Manager, Apple Music, Apple Store, Sign In with Apple, Apple Card. As of 1:44 p.m., Apple Support had the most reports, with over 13,000 user complaints. Comments suggest that users cannot log into their iCloud accounts, Apple Accounts, or activate devices, among other issues.

According to Apple, the disruptions aren't quite as widespread: Apple says that the App Store, Apple Music, AppleCare on Devices, and Schoolwork are all experiencing outages. Apple says that the App Store and Apple Music "may be slow or unavailable," while AppleCare purchase is currently unavailable. The company's System Status page shows an "issue" with iCloud Account & Sign In. Other services with user reports on Downdetector, including the Apple Card, Apple Online Store, and Apple Business, read as "Available." Apple also says there was an outage with the Volume Purchase Program, but that has since been resolved.

It's not clear what's causing the issues with the App Store, Apple Music, iCloud Account & Sign In, or other Apple services at this time. However, the timing is odd. It comes after a number of banks experienced outages on Monday, as well as Microsoft's massive outage the previous week. In addition to all of these outages, the FAA unexpectedly grounded all U.S. flights on Friday, for only the third time in the agency's history.
